articles.title: Good Nuclear, Bad Nuclear
articles.body:
Good Nuclear, Bad Nuclear
Europe's nuclear hypocrisy: Why is Iran expected to remain defenceless?
TEHRAN- After decades of lecturing Iran over its nuclear programme, European powers are embracing nuclear deterrence, participating in simulated nuclear warfare and even contemplating the development of their own atomic weapons. The question is no longer simply whether Iran's nuclear programme is peaceful, but why the rules of international security appear to apply differently to Tehran and European capitals.
For decades, European governments have positioned themselves as guardians of nuclear non-proliferation, repeatedly questioning Iran's nuclear ambitions, imposing political and economic pressure, and demanding restrictions on its nuclear programme. Yet, as Europe increasingly prepares for a potential nuclear confrontation and considers expanding its own nuclear capabilities, an uncomfortable question emerges: by what logic can European countries claim the right to pursue nuclear deterrence while denying Iran the right to determine the means of safeguarding its own security?
A recent report by "German Foreign Policy", published on October 15 under the headline "Europe, a nuclear-armed continent", offers a revealing account of this apparent contradiction. It describes an accelerating trend towards the militarisation of Europe's security architecture, including participation in nuclear warfare exercises, discussions about deploying additional American nuclear weapons on European soil, and renewed calls for Germany and other European countries to consider developing their own nuclear weapons.
The developments expose not only Europe's changing security priorities but also the profound double standards underpinning its longstanding approach to Iran's nuclear programme.
The hypocrisy of Europe's nuclear double standards
For years, European governments have been at the forefront of international efforts to restrict Iran's nuclear programme, frequently invoking concerns that Tehran might eventually seek to develop nuclear weapons. These accusations have provided political justification for sanctions, diplomatic pressure and repeated attempts to impose additional restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities.
Yet the same European capitals are now moving in a remarkably different direction when it comes to their own nuclear ambitions.
According to German Foreign Policy, Germany is participating in NATO's annual Steadfast Noon nuclear warfare exercise, alongside 16 other NATO members. The exercise involves operational preparations for the simulated deployment of nuclear bombs. The Bundeswehr is also participating for the first time in France's nuclear exercise, Operation Poker.
Meanwhile, Finland has moved to remove its longstanding legal prohibition on hosting or transporting nuclear weapons, while Lithuania is pursuing a similar constitutional change. Discussions about potentially stationing American nuclear weapons in Poland have also gained momentum.
 
Perhaps even more significant is the growing debate over an independent European nuclear weapons capability. German foreign policy circles have begun openly discussing the possibility of a German or jointly developed European nuclear arsenal, potentially involving Scandinavian and Baltic countries.
The contrast is striking. When Iran develops its nuclear technology under international safeguards, European governments portray it as a potential threat to international security. When European countries expand their nuclear military cooperation and contemplate acquiring additional nuclear capabilities, the same developments are presented as legitimate responses to security concerns.
If nuclear capabilities are inherently destabilising when pursued by Iran, why do they suddenly become instruments of stability when pursued by European countries?
Security for Europe, insecurity for Iran?
The underlying contradiction goes beyond nuclear policy. It reflects a broader European understanding of international security in which some countries are considered entitled to strengthen their deterrence capabilities, while others are expected to accept limitations on their security choices.
French President Emmanuel Macron's declaration in March that Europe was entering a new "age of nuclear weapons" is particularly revealing. His proposed advanced deterrence concept involves the possible temporary deployment of French nuclear-capable Rafale aircraft at bases in other European countries. The objective, according to the report, is to create uncertainty for potential adversaries and complicate their military calculations.
In other words, Europe increasingly views nuclear deterrence as an essential component of its security.
Germany, meanwhile, is questioning whether dependence on American nuclear protection is sufficient. Political scientist Joachim Krause, a former head of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, has argued that Germany should consider its own or European nuclear weapons. He has even suggested that possessing an atomic bomb would provide Germany with an additional element of security.
This raises a fundamental question: if nuclear deterrence is considered necessary for Germany's protection, why should Iran be expected to surrender every option that could contribute to its national security?
Iran operates in a considerably more volatile security environment than most European countries. It faces decades of American sanctions, persistent military threats, repeated acts of sabotage, assassinations of its officials and scientists, and direct military attacks involving the United States and Israel. Its geographical neighbourhood is also characterised by extensive foreign military deployments and the presence of nuclear-armed states.
These are not abstract security concerns. They are part of Iran's recent experience.
European governments cannot reasonably expect Tehran to disregard these realities while simultaneously embracing the argument that their own deteriorating security environment justifies greater reliance on nuclear weapons.
Security cannot be treated as an exclusive privilege reserved for powerful countries. Nor can the principle of deterrence be considered legitimate for one group of nations and inherently unacceptable for another.
Why is Iran expected to accept a different set of rules?
Perhaps the most important question raised by Europe's nuclear shift concerns the future of the international non-proliferation regime itself.
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) establishes obligations concerning the prevention of nuclear weapons proliferation, the peaceful use of nuclear energy and progress towards nuclear disarmament. Iran, as a non-nuclear-weapon state party to the treaty, has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is intended for peaceful purposes and that it is entitled to develop nuclear technology under the treaty's provisions.
The European powers, meanwhile, have increasingly embraced nuclear deterrence as an indispensable instrument of their own security. France and the United Kingdom already possess nuclear arsenals, while several other European NATO members participate in nuclear-sharing arrangements involving American weapons.
The problem is not simply that Europe possesses nuclear weapons or participates in deterrence arrangements. It is that European governments continue to approach the nuclear question through a framework that appears to grant themselves considerable strategic flexibility while demanding increasingly restrictive commitments from Iran.
The disparity becomes even more difficult to justify when the respective security environments are considered.
Iran faces threats from countries that possess overwhelming conventional military capabilities and, in the case of Israeli regime, an undeclared nuclear arsenal. It has also experienced direct military aggression from the United States and Israel. Meanwhile, European countries are increasingly citing the possibility of a confrontation with Russia as justification for strengthening their nuclear deterrence.
If the prospect of a potential conflict is sufficient to justify expanding Europe's nuclear capabilities, how can Iran's much more immediate and tangible security concerns be dismissed?
And if nuclear weapons are being presented as the ultimate guarantee of sovereignty and national survival, what alternative security guarantees are actually being offered to countries such as Iran?
A dangerous lesson for the international order
Europe's evolving nuclear posture sends a deeply troubling message to the rest of the world: international rules and non-proliferation commitments can be interpreted flexibly when the security interests of powerful countries are at stake.
This approach risks undermining the very international framework that European governments have repeatedly invoked in their dealings with Iran. It also raises serious questions about the credibility of European diplomacy and its ability to act as an impartial participant in negotiations over nuclear issues.
Ultimately, the issue is not whether Iran should acquire nuclear weapons. The right to peaceful nuclear technology, the question of nuclear weapons acquisition, and the broader right of every nation to defend its sovereignty are separate matters that should not be deliberately conflated.
The real question is why Europe believes it can determine the security requirements of other nations while reserving for itself the freedom to pursue whatever military capabilities it considers necessary.
If nuclear deterrence is a legitimate response to insecurity, then European governments must explain why Iran's security concerns deserve less consideration than their own. If nuclear militarisation is dangerous and destabilising, they must apply that principle consistently, rather than using it selectively as a political instrument against countries they regard as adversaries.
Europe cannot spend decades demanding that Iran demonstrate restraint while simultaneously preparing for a nuclear confrontation of its own.
The world cannot be expected to accept a system in which the powerful are entitled to pursue nuclear deterrence, while the less powerful are told that their security must depend on the goodwill of those same powers.

articles.title: Israel ready to strike Iran with US, but specific joint goals remain unclear, source tells 'Post'
articles.body:
The IDF is ready to strike Iran if US President Donald Trump asks it to join the American air force in an operation after the November 3 midterm elections, but a wide cloud of uncertainty is hovering over the situation, The Jerusalem Post understands.
Part of what is making this attack more likely after Trump pulled out of prior threats to attack in August, earlier in October, and at other times in 2026 is that other methods have been tried to obtain Iranian concessions and some of Trump’s team is shifting back toward attacking, the Post has learned.
At earlier points in the war, and in August and October, many of his top advisers, including, critically, sometimes US Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, were skeptical about the utility of attacking. There are sources who push back on this and some of the below characterizations of positions of Trump officials regarding the conflict with Iran.
At certain times, Caine and others were also more worried about a lack of readiness in terms of interceptors, defense capabilities for US forces and allies in the region, and the placement of critical military assets.
Trump and many of his non-military advisors were also worried about the impact of an additional round with Iran, which is hugely unpopular in the US, on the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections.
But once the midterms pass – and with Caine now shifting gears to believing Iran will not meet the US president’s minimum goals regarding the nuclear and Strait of Hormuz standoffs absent additional military pressure – the main bars to the use of force will have been removed, according to sources. There are those who push back on attempts to characterize the US military as having shifted, concerned that this could be to further an over-aggressive agenda.
US increases military presence in Israel, Middle East
Over the past week, more than 10 US military transport aircraft arrived at the Nevatim and Uvda air force bases in the South, seeming to set the table for a serious operation.
There have also been reports of US air defense systems and interceptors being moved to Israel and to other Arab allies.
But there are still fewer US forces in the region than there were in previous periods.
Yet, this is only the starting point.
There are disagreements between the US and Israel about what the goals of such an operation would be.
Mossad, IDF appear to disagree on targets of renewed fighting with Iran
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continues to talk about regime change, and Mossad Director Roman Gofman is working hard on plans to advance that goal, according to sources.
In contrast, the IDF’s focus tends to be on specific threat reduction items.
These could include the Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility, some kind of attempt to reduce the threat that the regime could recover its 60% highly enriched uranium under the rubble of three previously bombed nuclear sites, any newly opened sites relating to the weapons group, new or repaired ballistic missile production sites, and strategic weapons, such as possibly space-related weapons.
Top Israeli officials have also publicly threatened to strike Iran’s top energy facilities.
It is unclear whether they will include assassinations of top Iranian officials, given that Israel has killed dozens of top Iranian officials twice since June 2025, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and other top figures in the regime maintained a hardline stance afterwards.
There has been less public discussion about targeting Mojtaba Khamenei, the son of the ayatollah, and the regime’s current ruler.
Key goal for US is keeping any conflict short
Trump is much more focused on achieving some concessions on the nuclear issue and opening Hormuz.
Even in the past Iran operations, the US avoided assassinating top Iranian officials.
Next, US officials are highly concerned about keeping any new operation against Iran time-limited, possibly as short as a few days.
In contrast, even if Israeli officials do not want another 40-day war, they also have not talked about keeping the operation as short as Washington has emphasized.
Trump’s public comments have focused on sending a brief message to Iran to advance nuclear negotiations.
Israeli officials’ public comments have emphasized bringing a longer-term end to the threats posed by Tehran by using extensive kinetic force.
US Joint Chiefs Chairman concerned short campaign won't achieve Trump's goals
Caine remains worried about Iran pushing the war for longer than Trump wants – the regime does not need to stop firing ballistic missiles all over the region just because the US stops bombing, the Post understands.
But, according to sources, Caine believes this risk must be swallowed given the absence of any sign that Iran will cut a deal at any discernible point simply based on economic pressure.
He is not at all sure that another short military campaign will get to Trump’s goals, but believes it is one of the last things left to try, the Post understands.
Caine also remains firmly against trying to achieve regime change, which he still believes is a pipe dream – at least at this stage, regardless of the harm that America can inflict on the Iranian economy.
Spokesperson for the Office of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Joseph Holstead responded, “We do not discuss the chairman’s confidential conversations with the president, the secretary of war, or other senior leaders, nor do we comment on anonymous, agenda-driven characterizations of those conversations by sources who were not privy to them.
“The chairman provides the president, secretary of war, and National and Homeland Security Councils with his best military advice and recommendations, along with all associated risks, candidly and confidentially,” he added.
The Post sought comment from the Pentagon, which referred to General Caine's office, and the White House, from which it had not yet received a response at press time.

articles.title: North Korea tests cluster-bomb warhead for ballistic missiles
articles.body:
- North Korea tested a “Standard Type 2” cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31, claiming it can destroy 12 to 13 hectares.
- The Missile Administration said units will be able to use four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year.
North Korea tested a cluster-bomb warhead for its tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31 and said it will let its military units choose from four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year, state news agency KCNA reported on Nov. 1.
The Missile Administration, which runs North Korea’s missile development, said the test assessed the warhead’s combat readiness and destructive power. Its Ballistic Missile System Institute and Warhead Institute said they confirmed that the “Standard Type 2” cluster warhead can destroy a target area of 12 to 13 hectares, about 30 to 32 acres. Kim Jong Sik, a member of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Central Military Commission and first vice director of a Central Committee department, oversaw the test. Leader Kim Jong Un was not reported to have attended.
KCNA did not name the missile or give its range, altitude or launch site. The missile was fired at an uninhabited island target in the West Sea, also known as the Yellow Sea, South Korea’s JKN reported, and analysts said it appears to be the first time North Korea has fired a cluster-armed missile from a wheeled mobile launcher.
“We classify the cluster-bomb warheads into four categories according to special and standard purposes. Within this year we will enable units to select and use all those types according to operational aims and specific features of targets,” said the general director of the DPRK Missile Administration.
A cluster warhead opens in the air and scatters dozens or hundreds of small bomblets over a wide area, making it effective against troops, vehicles, artillery positions and airfields rather than a single hardened target. Neither North Korea nor South Korea has joined the international convention banning cluster munitions.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launch on the day it happened, a break from its usual practice of reporting North Korean ballistic missile launches in real time. The military said on Nov. 1 that it had tracked related activity before the launch in close information sharing with the United States and maintained a readiness posture. Because the missile flew a short range at low altitude, the military wanted to complete its analysis before confirming it was a ballistic missile, Financial News reported.
North Korea has tested cluster warheads on its tactical missiles before. In April, it tested a Hwasong-11A short-range ballistic missile with a cluster warhead alongside other new weapons, and later that month Kim Jong Un watched the launch of Hwasong-11 Ra missiles fitted with cluster bomb and fragmentation mine warheads, which state media also claimed could devastate an area of about 13 hectares.
The test came two days after North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area during a firepower demonstration tied to a drone exhibition, where Kim called for “absolute superiority” in drone technology. The Missile Administration described the Oct. 31 launch as part of regular research work to improve the power of its weapon systems.

articles.title: Trump ‘checks in’ with Netanyahu amid fears of renewed hostilities – WSJ
articles.body:
Trump ‘checks in’ with Netanyahu amid fears of renewed hostilities – WSJ
US President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday morning, checking in amid preparations for possible strikes on Iran, the Wall Street Journal has reported, citing people familiar with the call.
According to the WSJ, Trump had earlier held another meeting with senior military commanders at the White House to discuss options for resuming major combat operations. Over the past few weeks, multiple media outlets have reported that the US could resume strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb Iran, warning of “another little Epic Fury” if Tehran fails to meet his peace terms. US officials have reportedly warned Arab allies hosting American military bases to prepare for a short but intense operation.
Asked at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago in Florida on Saturday night whether he expected to “go back to war with Iran” in the coming weeks, Trump replied: “Let’s say I did – would I tell you? I can’t tell you this.”
The Pentagon has reportedly presented Trump with potential targets ranging from Iranian nuclear facilities and underground military sites to Kharg Island, a major oil export hub in the Persian Gulf. The US has also been sending additional missile interceptors to the region and relocating troops from vulnerable bases.
According to a Jerusalem Post report published on Saturday, the US and Israel have already drawn up plans for renewed military action, but Trump is unlikely to order strikes before Tuesday’s vote unless intelligence indicates preparations for a surprise attack.
A resumption of hostilities would come at a sensitive time for Netanyahu, whose right-wing bloc failed to secure a parliamentary majority in last week’s election. He will remain in office as coalition negotiations continue.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump had not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran but preferred a diplomatic solution. His remarks came as Iranian negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha following more than 12 hours of discussions in Tehran on Friday. A source familiar with the talks told Reuters that diplomacy was being coordinated through regular contacts with Washington.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had reviewed a letter from US Vice President J.D. Vance aimed at reopening negotiations, describing the initiative as a “positive step.”
Meanwhile, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered the armed forces to prepare for “an immediate and effective response, without geographical restriction” if the country is attacked again, according to a statement released by his office on Saturday.

articles.title: Israel completes 'preparations' for Iran confrontation as US weighs options — report
articles.body:
Israel has completed preparations for a renewed military attack on Iran, whilst US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper has presented President Donald Trump with military options for resuming attacks, the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported.
“The Israeli military has finalised defensive and offensive readiness for a potential return to combat, though any decision to launch an offensive remains with Trump as diplomatic contacts continue.”
Citing unnamed political sources, the daily reported that Israel is approaching another round of fighting, but its leadership cannot unilaterally initiate the campaign, which hinges on whether Washington pursues an agreement with Tehran or orders coordinated strikes.
Preparations have advanced beyond planning.
The Israeli air force has carried out multiple long-range drills involving dozens of fighter jets and mid-air refuelling tankers across Syrian and Iraqi airspace towards Iranian frontiers to rehearse potential strike corridors.
Strategic dilemmas
Cooper tabled strike plans during a White House briefing attended by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine, though no order to resume combat has been given.
In recent days, 10 US military transport aircraft have landed at Israeli airbases delivering equipment, coinciding with broader American force reinforcements.
Sources noted a fundamental strategic dilemma: the lack of clearly defined US operational objectives.
Striking Iranian nuclear facilities, missile infrastructure, and military assets would not guarantee government collapse or policy shifts, though Washington could leverage threats to extract concessionary terms.
Regional escalation remains a critical hazard, with officials warning Hezbollah could enter the fray, stretching Israeli air defences and interceptor stockpiles.
Concurrently, indirect contacts mediated by Qatar continue, exploring prospective terms regarding Iran's nuclear programme, the Strait of Hormuz, and economic incentives, with Russia and China as potential guarantors.
Hostilities originally erupted on February 28, following joint US-Israeli strikes, before an April truce broke down into renewed exchanges in July amid stalled diplomacy.

articles.title: Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
articles.body:
Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
TEHRAN - In the new international order, the concept of “power” is no longer defined solely by the number of nuclear warheads, overseas military bases, or classical security alliances; rather, the new geometry of global power is shaped by the capacity of supply chains, currency exchanges, infrastructure investments, and economic interdependence.
Within this novel framework, China has managed to elevate its position from a mere trading power in the late twentieth century to a “structural actor in international crisis management”—an actor whose primary tools for intervening in crises are not missiles and sanctions, but economic integration and financial leverage.
The defining distinction of China’s approach to international crises is rooted in the theory of “developmental peace” as opposed to Western “liberal peace.” Beijing believes that the primary root of many geopolitical conflicts and security instabilities in the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia lies not in a vacuum of Western democracy, but in poverty, a deficit of infrastructural development, and a lack of connection to global markets. Therefore, Beijing utilizes initiatives such as the Belt and Road and strategic energy partnerships as efficient tools to contain security shocks. When countries share tangible, mutual economic interests in the continuity of joint projects, the cost of escalating tensions and war increases dramatically for them.
A concrete and successful example of this strategy can be seen in Beijing’s historic mediation between Tehran and Riyadh. Leveraging its immense weight as the largest buyer of Persian Gulf energy and the primary trading partner of both countries, China provided an economic-strategic platform for a political agreement without the need for ideological alignments. This model demonstrated that Beijing’s crisis management levers are built on a commitment to mutual interests and non-interference in internal affairs—a factor that has made Beijing’s model attractive and acceptable among the countries of the Global South.
Furthermore, in complex crises such as the war in Ukraine or tensions surrounding maritime security, China has managed—by relying on its position as a core commodity buyer—to prevent devastating fractures in the global energy and food markets. China’s policy is to maintain a balance between trade with Russia while simultaneously safeguarding Western markets; a strategy that prevents the deepening of acute international deadlocks and the uncontrolled spread of crises into the global economy.
Ultimately, Beijing has demonstrated that economic power is not merely a source of wealth, but a decisive lever for containing shocks and moderating geopolitical behavior. Although China’s cautious policy and avoidance of direct security guarantees may appear to limit its role in certain acute crises, an undeniable reality remains: in the current post-hegemonic world, no major international crisis can be managed, sustainably resolved, or contained without considering Beijing’s capacities, considerations, and economic levers.
*Mahdi Zolfaghari is an associate professor in the Department of Asian Studies at Allameh Tabataba’i University

articles.title: Greece receives second FDI frigate HS Nearchos
articles.body:
- Naval Group delivered HS Nearchos, Greece’s second FDI frigate, at Lorient on Oct. 30, ten months after the first ship, HS Kimon.
- The third Greek frigate is due by the end of 2026, and a fourth, ordered in November 2025, is scheduled for 2028.
Naval Group handed over HS Nearchos, the second of Greece’s new French-built defense and intervention frigates, to the Hellenic Navy at its shipyard in Lorient, France, on Oct. 30, ten months after Greece received the first ship of the class.
Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias and French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin attended the ceremony. The third Greek frigate, HS Formion, is due by the end of 2026, which would give the Hellenic Navy three of the ships within a year, the company said. Naval Group did not say when Nearchos will sail for Greece or enter operational service.
“Only ten months after the delivery of HS Kimon, it is an honour to deliver the second FDI frigate for the Hellenic Navy, HS Nearchos, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin and Nikos Dendias, whom I would like to thank for their renewed trust,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The FDI, short for Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention, is a French design of about 4,500 tons and 122 m (400 feet) built for air defense, anti-ship and anti-submarine warfare. Greece’s version, known as the FDI HN or Kimon class, carries a heavier weapons fit than the French Navy’s ships, with Thales Sea Fire radar and up to 32 Aster 30 long-range air defense missiles. Greece is also buying Schiebel CAMCOPTER S-100 drones to fly from Kimon, Nearchos and Formion for surveillance and anti-submarine work.
The first ship, HS Kimon, was delivered on Dec. 18, 2025, and arrived in Greece in January. In March, Greece sent it to Cyprus to help defend the island against Iranian attacks, alongside a Hydra-class frigate and F-16 fighters, its first operational mission. At the time, Kimon was the only Greek warship able to provide long-range air defense, Naval News reported.
Greece agreed in September 2021 to buy three of the frigates, with an option for a fourth, in a package worth about €3 billion including weapons, and the program started in 2022. It exercised the option in November 2025, ordering a fourth ship, HS Themistokles, along with maintenance and upgrades for the whole fleet. That ship is due in 2028.
More than 75 Greek companies are involved in Naval Group’s frigate and submarine programs for Greece, supplying parts ranging from electronic maps to pre-outfitted hull blocks and complex mechanical and electronic systems, the company said. Naval Group has committed to 25% local content on the fourth frigate. It has also won the initial in-service support contract for the Greek FDIs, which it will carry out with its Greek subsidiary, Naval Group Hellas, and local partners.
The Greek ships are part of a larger order book. Thirteen FDIs have now been ordered for three NATO navies, five for France, four for Greece and four for Sweden, and Naval Group says its Lorient yard can now deliver two of the frigates a year.

articles.title: Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
articles.body:
Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
- North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers are blamed for a record US$6 billion Binance crypto theft. US authorities say the group is linked to Lazarus and Pyongyang’s cyber warfare programme.
- TraderTraitor uses fake job offers and malware to steal data and digital assets. The FBI says hackers have also hit DMM Bitcoin, Atomic Wallet, Alphapo, CoinsPaid and Bybit.
- Stolen crypto is laundered through mixing services and private exchanges, then used for weapons research and procurement. Analysts say cybercrime gives North Korea fast money despite sanctions.
AI generated
SEOUL – North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group has been blamed by the US authorities for stealing more than US$6 billion (S$7.7 billion) in virtual assets from Binance, in what is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history.
The Oct 29 attack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyberthefts linked to Pyongyang, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons programme.
Here are five things to know about the group and its place in North Korea’s cyberwarfare programme:
Who are they?
TraderTraitor is the name given to a North Korean hacking operation linked to the broader Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it hacked Sony Pictures in retaliation for The Interview, a satirical film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Pyongyang has invested heavily in developing its cybercapabilities since at least the mid-1990s, building a force that South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 comprised around 8,400 personnel.
“North Korea has built a capable cyberforce, funnelling many of the country’s top students into computer science and IT training,” the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on its website.
Much of the hacking activity is known to have been directed by Pyongyang’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, its primary foreign intelligence agency.
“The top two students in my class were recruited to the hacking unit,” South Korean MP Park Choong-kwon, who studied at the North’s elite National Defense University before his defection, told AFP in a 2024 interview.
How do they operate?
TraderTraitor actors have been known to pose as recruiters offering lucrative jobs to trick victims into downloading malicious software.
The malware can allow hackers to infiltrate victims’ computer systems and steal sensitive information and digital assets.
In a 2024 heist involving the theft of US$308 million from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange DMM Bitcoin, a North Korean hacker posing as a recruiter on LinkedIn contacted an employee of a separate virtual currency wallet software company.
They sent the employee what appeared to be a pre-employment test, which actually contained a malicious line of code.
That allowed the hacker to compromise their system and impersonate the employee, the FBI said.
What have North Korean hackers done?
High-profile cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers include the theft of US$81 million from Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016 and the WannaCry ransomware attack that disrupted computers worldwide in 2017.
In 2022, the US authorities blamed Lazarus-linked hackers for stealing some US$620 million from the Ronin blockchain network.
The FBI subsequently attributed three more cryptocurrency heists in 2023 to TraderTraitor actors, involving the theft of nearly US$200 million from Atomic Wallet, AlphaPo and Coinspaid.
The scale of the thefts increased dramatically in February 2025, when the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing around US$1.5 billion in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit.
“TraderTraitor actors are proceeding rapidly and have converted some of the stolen assets,” the FBI said at the time.
How does North Korea use stolen funds?
The North Korean regime launders stolen cryptocurrency and converts it into cash “through mixing services or private exchanges”, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
“The proceeds are then channelled directly into military research, the illicit procurement of weapons components and the defence industry,” he added.
A 2024 United Nations report said proceeds from North Korean cyberattacks “reportedly helped to fund the country’s development of weapons of mass destruction”.
Why cybercrime?
Analysts say Pyongyang’s illicit cyberactivity is driven by its ability to obtain vast sums of money quickly and at “minimal cost”.
“While international sanctions severely restrict North Korea’s ability to earn foreign currency through conventional trade, cybertheft allows it to acquire billions of dollars with minimal personnel and resources,” said Lim.
“Hacking offers Pyongyang a way to obtain funds outside conventional banking channels, taking advantage of the pseudonymous and borderless nature of digital assets to bypass financial restrictions,” he added. 
AFP

articles.title: Iran’s army warns that any new war with US could be ‘longer than previous conflict’
articles.body:
Iran warns new war could last longer after Trump threatens strikes
- Iran warned a new war with the US could last longer than the last one. Army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Trump would not control how it ends.
- Defence Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi promised a “proportionate, decisive, and impactful response” to any attack. He said threats would not set Iran’s reply.
- IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said conflict with America has “no geographical limitations”. Trump said the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military and could hit more targets quickly.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran warned on Nov 1 that any new war with the United States could last longer than the previous round of fighting after President Donald Trump said he still had to “take care” of more targets.
Diplomatic efforts to end the Middle East war have been punctuated by repeated threats from the US and Israel to resume bombardments as they hold crucial elections.
“A potential future war could last longer than (the) previous conflict, and the American President would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion,” said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
He was referring to the most intense phase of the fighting in the war that began on Feb 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, killing the Islamic republic’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Iran responded by launching missiles and drones across the region, while the militant groups it backs also entered the fray in Lebanon and Yemen.
Iran’s Defence Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi on Nov 1 warned of a “proportionate, decisive, and impactful response” to any attack on the country, according to state TV.
“Those who pose threats will not dictate the scope, timing, or consequences of Iran’s defensive response,” he added.
Also on Nov 1, Hossein Mohebbi, the spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, echoed the remarks made by the country’s new supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in a written message the day before.
“In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy,” Mohebbi said, according to state TV.
Trump said on Oct 31 that the US has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets.
“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters at his Florida residence.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said “we hope the other side will exercise rationality and choose diplomacy”, adding that Iran “remains prepared for both defence and diplomacy”, according to the official IRNA news agency.
The warnings came as Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei disclosed on Oct 31 that he had received a letter from US Vice-President J.D. Vance seeking to revive talks.
He noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
He said Tehran had previously told Washington that unless its conditions were met, “neither would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened nor would there be any negotiations”.
Those conditions include unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, ending the months-long US naval blockade of Iranian ports, lifting longstanding sanctions and ending the war on all fronts.
Since the war began, Iran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, and repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to cross without its authorisation.
The US has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
‘Braced for the worst’
Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, said on Nov 1 that the United Arab Emirates hoped that the exchanges would yield a breakthrough but was preparing for the worst.
“We’re hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough,” he told a conference in Manama, Bahrain.
“It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we’re also, as we’ve shown before, braced for the worst.”
In Tehran, some residents described a sense of helplessness as threats of renewed fighting mount.
“The news coming in is truly worrying. However, no matter how much I, as an ordinary citizen, immerse myself in these reports, there is nothing I can actually do about it,” Mohadese, a 27-year-old health inspector, told AFP.
Others including 48-year-old vendor Ebrahim saw no reason to be concerned.
“We do not fear another war; we have been at war for 48 years now – we are always at war,” he said in downtown Tehran. AFP

articles.title: North Korea Tests Hwasong-11D Ballistic Missile With Cluster Warhead
articles.body:
On October 31, North Korea tested a Hwasong-11D tactical ballistic missile equipped with a conventional cluster warhead.
North Korea’s state news agency KCNA reported the test.
According to the agency, the Missile Administration conducted the test to assess the combat capabilities and destructive power of the cluster warhead fitted to an unnamed tactical ballistic missile.
The test reportedly confirmed that a standard Type 2 cluster warhead could “turn an area of 12–13 hectares with an extremely high density of strikes into scorched earth.”
The head of the Missile Administration said special-purpose and standard-type cluster warheads were divided into four categories and that, this year, every unit could select and use them according to its operational requirements and the characteristics of the targets to be destroyed.
Joseph Dempsey, a research associate for defense and military analysis at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, noted that the released images indicate that the missile used in the test was a Hwasong-11D ballistic missile.
Its relatively short range and the fact that it was fired toward an island off North Korea’s west coast used as a test range (38.720234, 125.114059) explain why Japan and South Korea did not issue prior reports of the launch.
Based on the island’s dimensions, the impact area of the cluster submunitions was approximately 380-390 meters long and 250–260 meters wide, covering 7.5-8 hectares. This is significantly smaller than the claimed 12-13 hectares.
The Hwasong-11D, also known as the Hwasongpho-11Ra, is a North Korean tactical ballistic missile. Experts consider it a scaled-down version of the Hwasong-11A, also known as the KN-23. Its first known test launches took place on April 16, 2022, when North Korea presented the system as a new tactical guided weapon for forward artillery units.
According to estimates by the Korea Defense and Security Forum (KODEF), the missile is approximately 4.5 meters long and 600 mm in diameter.
During tests in April 2022, the missiles traveled approximately 110 km, reached an altitude of about 25 km, and attained speeds of up to Mach 4. In May 2024, the South Korean military recorded a flight range of approximately 300 km.
The initial version of the missile is believed to use an inertial navigation system with satellite correction. In May 2024, North Korea announced a test of a new “autonomous” navigation system but did not disclose further details.
The system’s basic mobile launcher uses a wheeled chassis and carries four missiles in rectangular transport and launch containers. On August 4, 2024, a ceremony in Pyongyang handed over 250 such launchers to the Korean People’s Army.

articles.title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as drones damage Russian facility
articles.body:
Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as drones damage Russian facility
- Russian strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians in four regions, while Ukraine said it hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, linked to missile production.
- Nizhny Novgorod governor Gleb Nikitin said a Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial site, and fuel officials warned against “panic buying”.
- Both sides kept up long-range attacks despite a local ceasefire near Oleshky. Russia said it downed 235 drones, while Ukraine said it shot down 371 of 433 Russian drones.
AI generated
KYIV – Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power on Nov 1, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, while the Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.
Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no let-up in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelensky said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
Moscow did not comment on the reported attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Overall, Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. Ukraine’s air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since the evening of Oct 31.
In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as at the morning of Nov 1. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.
Fuel supplies
Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government also did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to “buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying”, Interfax reported.
The warning suggests the damaged facility was linked to the region’s oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
On Oct 30, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.
In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Nov 1, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the energy sector, did not mention the Nizhny Novgorod strike, but said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices. articles.title: North Korea tests cluster warhead for tactical ballistic missile
articles.body:
North Korea conducted a test of a cluster warhead for a tactical ballistic missile to assess its combat applicability and destructive power, state media reported on Sunday.
The Missile Administration carried out the test on Saturday, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The test was overseen by General Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and first deputy director of a department of the party's Central Committee.
North Korea's Ballistic Missile Systems Research Institute and Warhead Research Institute said the test confirmed that the country's "Type-2 standard cluster warhead" could devastate a target area of about 12 to 13 hectares (29 to 32 acres) at what they described as an "ultra-high density."
The head of the Missile Administration said North Korea classifies its cluster warheads into four categories, including special-purpose and standard types.
He said Pyongyang plans to make all four types available to military units by the end of this year, allowing them to select warheads according to operational objectives and the characteristics of targets.
The Missile Administration described the test as part of regular scientific research aimed at increasing the destructive power of its weapons systems.

articles.title: NATO turns 5G towers into sensors in Baltic battlefield experiment
articles.body:
- NATO linked a Maven system to a national system in hours using agentic AI and ran a Lithuania-to-Latvia counter-drone engagement during DiBaX 2026.
- The Oct. 19-30 experiment in Latvia also tested military use of commercial 5G networks, jam-resistant communications and 5G-based object detection.
NATO linked a Maven targeting system to a national military system in a matter of hours using agentic artificial intelligence and ran a cross-border counter-drone engagement during a two-week experiment in Latvia, the alliance’s top transformation commander said on Oct. 30.
Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, described the results at Ādaži Military Base near Riga at the close of the Digital Backbone Experimentation, known as DiBaX 2026, which ran from Oct. 19 to 30. He said some tests failed along the way and that the alliance had deliberately accepted that risk.
“We have connected systems that were never designed to communicate with each other, using artificial intelligence to overcome interoperability barriers. It’s the first time that we have, for example, a Maven system that is speaking to a national system, and that has been fixed in hours with Agentic AI,” said Vandier.
NATO bought its own version of Palantir’s AI-enabled Maven Smart System in 2025 to help commanders pull together intelligence and speed up decisions, and has been rolling it out across its headquarters. Vandier did not say which country’s system Maven was connected to. Agentic AI refers to software that can carry out multistep tasks on its own, in this case working out how two systems exchange data.
The counter-drone test crossed a national border. A drone took off in Lithuania, flew into Latvia and was engaged there by a counter-drone system, Vandier said. It was one of several trials under NATO’s Layered Counter-UAS Initiative, which looks at how sensors and weapons from different countries and companies can work together as one layered defense against drones.
“Even if it didn’t work this morning, it has been done this week. So we had a drone taking off from Lithuania, arriving here and being engaged by a counter system,” said Vandier.
DiBaX itself tested three ways to keep NATO forces connected. In the first, organizers set up a private slice of a host country’s commercial 5G network, reserved and secured for military use, so arriving NATO forces could have command and data links from their first day before their own infrastructure arrived. The second tested automatic switching between communication paths when one is jammed, including radio across different frequencies, satellite links such as 5G direct-to-device, and troposcatter, which bounces radio signals off the lower atmosphere to reach beyond the horizon. The third used ordinary 5G cell towers as passive sensors to detect objects moving through their coverage, particularly in cities with dense tower networks. Vandier said a team of medics in the field also sent patient biodata over the network to doctors in the United States.
The scenarios were built around grey-zone incidents below the threshold of NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause, such as drone incursions and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. A third track, Next Generation Targeting, tested AI-enabled decision support to shorten the time between collecting information and acting on it, and Vandier said the targeting process ran noticeably faster by the end of the week than at the start.
“For us, as a NATO member of the Alliance Eastern Flank here in Latvia, we cannot afford to treat technological innovation and adaptation as a distant objective for us,” said Lt. Gen. Kaspars Pudāns, commander of the Latvian National Armed Forces.
Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, the United States, Canada, Finland and other allies took part, along with NATO bodies including the DIANA innovation accelerator and the NATO Communications and Information Agency. More than 60 technology companies joined, among them Ericsson, Nokia, Thales and Portuguese drone maker TEKEVER, with Latvian telecom company LMT acting as technical integrator. This was the fifth year in a row the experiment has been held in Latvia.
The event closed with NATO FUSE on Oct. 29 and 30, which included live field demonstrations. NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, visited Latvia on Oct. 30 and met President Edgars Rinkēvičs. European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis used the event to announce two pilot European Drone Technology Hubs, one in Latvia and one in the Netherlands, to open in 2027 and speed up development and testing of drone and counter-drone technology in cooperation with NATO.
“The next challenge, and it’s the most difficult, is adoption,” said Vandier.

articles.title: Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
articles.body:
Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has accused his political opponents of receiving support from an “army of Russian bots”amid an escalating constitutional crisis in Warsaw. The pro-EU leader offered no proof for his claim, which came after a government-backed judge moved to oust two key officials supported by his rival, right-wing President Karol Nawrocki, from the Constitutional Tribunal, triggering public outrage.
Unrest erupted on Friday when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge elected by Tusk’s governing majority, ordered the suspension of Constitutional Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski, both linked to the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. The tribunal’s existing leadership rejected the suspensions, declaring that all those participating in the attempted takeover “are committing the crime of a coup d’état.”
The development triggered street protests around the court building and a heavy police deployment. Nawrocki, who canceled a planned trip to Senegal, personally pushed his way into the tribunal to confront Korwin-Piotrowska and her allies, telling them that “you are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal.”
In a televised address on Saturday evening, Tusk scrambled to defend his actions, accusing his rivals of “seeking to destroy democracy and the rule of law.” The Polish PM, a strong supporter of EU integration who served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019, has long criticized PiS judicial reforms – which he said undermined judges’ independence – as well as Nawrocki’s refusal to administer the oath to five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
“Is it greed, stupidity or treason?” Tusk asked, claiming that the opposition was receiving support from “pro-Russian forces worldwide.”
“In this conflict, they’re using an army of Russian bots online. In fact, they’ve even received public compliments from the Kremlin’s chief ideologue,” the prime minister claimed, without providing further proof or elaborating.
Moscow has repeatedly said it does not interfere in other countries’ domestic affairs. While Russian officials have yet to respond to Tusk’s allegation, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov in July denied that Russia was responsible for cyberattacks on Polish energy infrastructure.
Responding to Tusk’s address, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, called the prime minister a “pathological liar” and accused him of setting Poland ablaze while pretending to extinguish the fire. “It’s hard to find a single word, expression, or sentence that would be true, that would reflect the actual or legal reality,” he added.
Tusk’s accusation comes after several Western media outlets, anti-Russia hawks, and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky propagated the claim that Kiev’s drone strikes, which damaged several data centers operated by Russian technology giant Yandex, crippled alleged Russian bot networks supporting Western right-wing movements, including Germany’s AfD and US President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.
However, several independent investigations by cybersecurity and research firms quickly debunked the narrative. Experts in particular pointed out that one viral graph supposedly showing a collapse in AfD-related activity was found to contain fabricated or unverifiable figures.
Commenting on the chaos, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev described it as a “constitutional coup.” He suggested that “Brussels’ protégé Tusk” was persecuting PiS conservatives over the latter’s hostility toward Ukrainian Nazi collaborators. Medvedev concluded by sarcastically invoking an old schoolyard joke, saying, “And these are the people who scold my brother and me for picking our noses.”

articles.title: Attack boats stayed in harbour all summer, report warns
articles.body:
Britain’s attack submarine fleet spent the summer tied up in harbour while Russian activity around British waters increased, and the availability of escorts for the ballistic missile boats that carry the nuclear deterrent is among the consequences raised, according to a briefing paper published by the 878 Institute.
The paper, the first in a planned series on the condition of the Royal Navy, opens by saying: “The Royal Navy is gripped by a critical but needless decline in strategic capacity, as demonstrated by a steep reduction in both mass and readiness.
“This comes at a time of intensifying maritime competition and growing threats to British national interests. These threats are most acute in and around British waters, as Russia’s submarines, warships and even its shadow-fleet carrying illicit Russian oil across the globe, are all increasing their operations off Britain’s coasts.”
It records that the Royal Navy spent twenty-one days in July alone monitoring Russian ships, that operations to track Russian activity rose twenty-five per cent on the previous year, and that Russian warships made repeated voyages through the Dover Strait and the North Sea. Ministers have confirmed that Moscow uses commercial proxies to threaten undersea infrastructure, and the paper cites analysis uncovering five hundred incidents of Russian civilian vessels loitering above cables.
Concerns about the frigate and destroyer fleets are set out alongside the navy’s transition to automation through the hybrid navy concept, before the paper turns to its main subject. It says: “However, it is in the submarine fleet that we see an especially stark vulnerability and where, due to its purposes, creates unique threats to Britain’s security.”
On the Astute class, which numbers five in service with two more being readied, the paper states: “Despite maintaining a fleet of five vessels, it was reported that not a single Astute-class submarine was operationally deployed through summer 2026, and that all five remained laid-up in British harbours. Only HMS Agamemnon (one of the two planned additions to the five in service) is at sea conducting trials.
“This is deeply concerning, given both the rise in Russian sub-surface activity around British waters, but perhaps more worrying because of the lack of available escorts for Britain’s nuclear deterrent.” That finding draws on reporting by Navy Lookout, and the Ministry of Defence does not comment on submarine operations.
Turning to the four Vanguard boats, the paper acknowledges that deployment cycles are not discussed publicly and then sets out what it describes as widely understood. It says: “Due to the nature of their deterrent, HM Government rightly does not comment on their deployment cycles or current state. However, it is widely understood that the fleet has been in a poor state for some years.”
Designed for patrols of three to four months, the boats have run planned patrols of under a hundred days well past that mark. The paper says: “Most SSN- and SSBN-operating navies view 100-day patrols as the sensible maximum; at least the last ten deterrent patrols all exceeded five months in duration, up until April this year, with the last coming in at over 200 days, apparently becoming the new normal.”
On the four Dreadnought boats due in the early 2030s, the paper argues that work on their successor cannot wait, since each is designed for thirty years of service and the build alone takes twenty. The Ministry of Defence accepted the Strategic Defence Review’s recommendation to begin early definition and requirement-setting during this parliamentary term, a pledge affirmed in July, and the paper says: “However, this pledge was only affirmed in July 2026, and there have been no major announcements since; with only two full Parliamentary years left before the next General Election must be called, the Government needs to properly commit to Dreadnought’s successor at the earliest opportunity.”
The sharpest warnings concern SSN-AUKUS, where steel cutting on the first British boat is scheduled at Barrow-in-Furness in 2027. The paper says: “Given the likely concurrent Astute and Dreadnought programmes, the sole UK submarine construction site in Barrow-in-Furness risks facing acute labour shortfalls as soon as SSN-AUKUS begins. In the meantime the site has added only about 500 workers against a required 2,500 to run the parallel Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS build lines.
“The projected build-timeframes for SSN-AUKUS are also deeply concerning. Astute-class boats averaged 128 months to build; SSN-AUKUS are projected to take only 18 months each. This feels unrealistic, and risks cost overruns, delays, supply-chain over-stretch, and potentially an even bigger ‘submarine gap’.”
Describing the programme as Pillar One of AUKUS and saying it must not fail, the paper adds: “However, without guarantees of resource from HM Government that are currently absent, and instead a vague pledge of total vessels built, a lack of political leadership and gaps in the defence-industrial base, Britain risks being the weak link in the partnership.”
Four recommendations follow, covering a firm commitment to twelve SSN-AUKUS boats at the spring Spending Review in 2027, increased resources for the Astute class to clear maintenance backlogs and dockyard constraints, a standing requirement for two of the five Astutes to be deployable and operational at all times, and the commissioning of the Dreadnought successor definition phase by the close of 2027.
The 878 Institute published a broader paper on British deterrence gaps in August, which UKDJ reported at the time, covering land, space and naval capability with a foreword by General the Lord Dannatt. The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain has allowed its under-ice submarine capability to lapse and that the department has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap in northern waters, and the Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise.

articles.title: Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
articles.body:
Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on U.S. military bases across the Middle East, according to a sweeping Wall Street Journal investigation that offers the fullest public picture yet of what the war on Iran has cost American forces in the region.
The Journal's analysis, drawing on satellite imagery, Iranian military statements and interviews with U.S. officials, identified 274 damaged structures at 24 installations with an American military presence during the war's first six months.
The investigation found that Iran increasingly targeted buildings where American troops live and sleep, showing an improved ability to sequence attacks and strike with greater precision.
While the Pentagon has priced the damage to bases at a minimum of $5 billion, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter cited by The Journal, a separate person briefed on the cost said the figure could reach as high as $15 billion.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies, which reviewed the Journal's findings on damaged buildings, estimated that reconstruction alone would top $4 billion, a figure that excludes replacing the equipment and systems housed inside.
Those repairs come on top of the war's overall cost, which stood at $47.1 billion as of Oct. 16, according to a document viewed by The Journal.
According to an Associated Press analysis, Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
The Journal also said the human toll has also mounted. More than 20 U.S. service members have died in activity related to the war since it began on Feb. 28, according to Defense Department data, and more than 400 were wounded before a temporary ceasefire collapsed in July. After that, the government stopped publishing casualty figures specific to the conflict.

articles.title: Ukraine flies the first drone rescues of wounded troops
articles.body:
Ukraine has carried out the world’s first medical evacuations by heavy uncrewed aircraft, lifting wounded soldiers out of positions that could not be reached from the ground, and is developing evacuation drones as a dedicated capability of its own, according to the Ukrainian defence ministry.
Brave1, the defence innovation cluster working with the Ministry of Defence, set the requirement in 2024 after working with the military to define what such an aircraft would have to do. The criteria given to the defence technology market were that the aircraft must reliably carry 130 kilograms over a distance of at least fifteen kilometres and must carry an integrated communication system with at least three alternative types to survive in an electronic warfare environment, with lidar, optical stabilisation and navigation that works without satellites listed as options.
The first of those evacuations took place in October, when an infantryman of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade was lifted out of a position the enemy had blocked. A Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 hexacopter built by a Brave1 participant flew the mission, an aircraft weighing 98 kilograms with a payload capacity of 130 kilograms, and it covered more than fifteen kilometres on the outbound leg.
Preparation ran to months and drew on the experience of the uncrewed ground vehicle company of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade. Equipment had been dropped to the soldier in advance and he had to secure himself to the aircraft’s winch without help, while adjacent units launched bomber drones to pull enemy interceptors away from the rescue aircraft.
A second system, Stargate, was built specifically for evacuation at the request of assault troops. It deploys in ten minutes, carries 150 kilograms at speeds up to 105 kilometres an hour and holds a medical module with a stretcher, and its software can plot a route and return to a safe area without help if navigation is completely jammed.
Assault troops of the CODE 9.2 regiment used it twice in a single week to bring out severely wounded soldiers from the grey zone five kilometres from the Russian border, where terrain, water obstacles and first person view drones ruled out any ground rescue. The aircraft flew nearly thirty kilometres each way and came back with the casualties aboard while under electronic attack, relying on artificial intelligence alone for navigation, with heavy strike drones suppressing enemy positions to cover the run.
Conventional casualty evacuation has become close to impossible along much of the front because the density of drone coverage turns any vehicle movement into a target, and uncrewed ground vehicles took over much of the work at the cost of speed. Survival after serious trauma depends heavily on reaching surgical care quickly, and a crawling robot moving along a mined route can take many hours to cover ground a helicopter would cross in minutes.
Ukraine’s Defence Procurement Agency has contracted three times as many uncrewed systems of all types this year as it did last year.

America is using negotiations to buy time
Strategic affairs analyst Saeed Leilaz examined the letter sent by J.D. Vance to Mohsen Rezaei in an interview with the Etemad newspaper. The timing of the letter is significant because it comes amid heightened political and economic uncertainty. Leilaz argues that although the letter has been presented as an attempt to revive negotiations, it is accompanied by warnings and threats against Iranian infrastructure.
After failing to achieve certain military objectives, Washington has shifted toward a strategy designed to gain time, reduce attention on Iran's leverage in the Strait of Hormuz, and prepare the ground for stronger future pressure if necessary. Iran should respond through a balanced strategy that combines deterrence and diplomacy. He emphasizes the importance of maintaining military readiness, strengthening economic resilience, removing domestic obstacles to economic growth, and supporting productive sectors of the economy. Diplomatic channels should remain open, and negotiations should continue in a careful and calculated manner.
Kayhan: Trump seeks to portray himself as a victim
In an article, Kayhan argued that the conflict involving Iran has generated significant difficulties for both the United States and Europe. Many observers view the consequences of the confrontation as costly and destabilizing. Political pressure has become particularly intense for Trump. Developments linked to the conflict, combined with domestic challenges and election-related concerns, have forced him to modify his public messaging. Whereas he previously suggested that the conflict would have only a limited impact on the United States, he is now placing greater emphasis on portraying America as a target rather than an initiator. The newspaper also highlights rising energy concerns and continuing volatility in global oil prices. According to its analysis, expectations that economic conditions would rapidly improve have not been fulfilled. As a result, Trump is attempting to shift responsibility for the crisis onto Iran while presenting himself as responding to Iranian actions. This change in rhetoric is a sign of political weakness.
Iran: Diplomacy remains the best path for crisis management
The Iran newspaper focused on Tehran's proposed seven-day initiative, which was reportedly delivered through intermediaries. The analysis presents the proposal as a possible framework for reducing tensions and creating conditions for renewed diplomacy. The initiative is based on a series of reciprocal and phased measures. It seeks to connect several objectives, including ending hostilities, easing restrictions, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and creating a pathway toward renewed nuclear negotiations. Supporters believe that linking these elements together could establish clearer expectations for both sides and reduce uncertainty. The newspaper argues that the proposal may help build trust by providing a structured roadmap rather than relying on general political commitments. It further suggests that the framework could serve as a starting point for broader crisis management and help prevent the continuation of a cycle of escalation and retaliation. However, the paper stresses that implementation depends on political will and the readiness of all parties to take corresponding steps. Without reciprocal action, even a well-designed proposal is unlikely to succeed.
Khorasan: Decoding Vance's approach
Khorasan examined the possible objectives behind Vance's communication with Iran. According to the newspaper, American officials are eager to secure a diplomatic achievement before Nov. 3 midterm elections and view an agreement with Tehran as politically valuable. Washington reportedly wants nuclear issues to be incorporated into any broader arrangement. Tehran, however, is unwilling to accept such conditions under the current circumstances. Because the exact contents of the message remain unclear, Khorasan focuses on the broader political implications. The newspaper identifies two possible tactics. The first involves highlighting particular negotiating figures in an attempt to exploit perceived domestic divisions within Iran. The second involves introducing new conditions that could replace or alter previous understandings reached between the parties. Despite these concerns, Khorasan emphasizes that Iran remains willing to engage in dialogue. Nevertheless, it argues that successful negotiations require changes in Washington's approach and greater attention to Iranian concerns and conditions.
Hamshahri: Response without geographical limitations
Hamshahri discussed a Saturday order from the Leader of the Islamic Revolution to the armed forces in the event of resumption of war against Iran by pointing to the views of regional affairs analyst Seyyed Morteza Mousavi. According to Mousavi, the order emphasized preparedness, deterrence, and the ability to respond rapidly to any future threat. He identified three main themes: maintaining full readiness, delivering immediate and effective responses to threats, and ensuring that Iran would determine the course and duration of any future confrontation if attacked. Mousavi argued that recent conflicts demonstrated the importance of deterrence and military readiness in shaping regional security calculations. He also stated that any country allowing its territory or facilities to be used in attacks against Iran could face consequences in the event of future hostilities. In his interpretation, the order was intended to signal determination that responses to future threats would not necessarily be confined to a specific geographical area.

articles.title: Fire Point confirmed the strike on the Kstovo Refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil refineries
