Fire Point confirmed the strike on the Kstovo Refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil refineries
Kyiv • UNN
A fire broke out at the NORSI refinery in Kstovo after a drone attack. The exact extent of the damage and the location of the strike are being determined.
During the night of November 1, the Defense Forces struck the Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez oil refinery in the city of Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod region—one of Russia’s largest refineries. This was reported on its Telegram channel by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, the manufacturer of FP-1 long-range attack drones, UNN writes.
Details
The company published the post on Sunday morning, playing on the Halloween phrase "trick or treat."
Kstovo Oil Refinery, trick or treat!
Fire Point had previously reported that the Defense Forces used FP-1 drones in earlier strikes on the Kstovo refinery, including on August 26.
Local residents reported a series of explosions in Kstovo during the night, after which a fire broke out on the plant’s premises—video footage appeared on social media at around 4 a.m. According to a preliminary assessment by the Exilenova+ monitoring channel, the fire may have started in the area of the AVT-5 and AVT-6 primary oil-refining units, the visbreaking unit for fuel oil, or the 35/11-600 unit. The exact strike location and extent of the damage have not yet been established.
Nizhny Novgorod Region Governor Gleb Nikitin said that the region had come under a "massive drone attack" during the night. According to him, an industrial facility in Kstovo District sustained significant damage.
What is known about the Kstovo refinery
"Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez" (NORSI) is Russia’s fourth-largest refinery by processing volume. Its designed capacity is approximately 17 million tonnes of oil per year, or about 340,000 barrels per day; according to the Special Operations Forces, the plant accounts for up to 11% of gasoline production in the Russian Federation. The facility produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, fuel oil, bitumen, and lubricants, and is one of the main fuel suppliers to the Moscow region. According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the plant is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian army.
Additionally
In 2026, the Kstovo refinery has already been attacked more than once. The Defense Forces struck it on May 18 and 20—after which, according to Reuters, the plant shut down its primary refining unit, which accounts for more than half of its capacity. On July 2, the General Staff confirmed that the plant had been struck, preliminarily identifying the AVT-6 unit; as UNN reported, weapons manufactured by Fire Point were used at the time. On August 26, FP-1 drones struck the refinery, and on September 4, the General Staff confirmed that the facility had ceased operations.
A few days ago, Fire Point also reported that FP-1 drones had struck the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Russia’s Samara region, whose designed capacity is approximately 8.8 million tonnes of oil per year.
We remind you
In September, following strikes by the Defense Forces, the operations of LUKOIL-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez LLC and NOVATEK-Ust-Luga in Russia were halted.

articles.title: Trump says US still has ‘one or two targets’ in Iran
articles.body:
Trump says US still has ‘one or two targets’ in Iran
- Trump said the US has destroyed much of Iran’s military and nuclear programme, but still has “one or two sites” to hit, including a suspected complex at Pickaxe Mountain.
- Iran warned of an “immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response” if attacked, while its leaders ordered new target lists and kept the Strait of Hormuz blockade in place.
- Diplomatic efforts continue through Qatar and Pakistan, but no deal has been reached. The conflict has lifted oil prices and could affect US and Israeli politics.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump said on Oct 31 that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
He said the US is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran’s military and nuclear programme.
“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” he told reporters at his Florida residence.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
The Iranian government denied any nuclear work is carried out there.
Earlier on Oct 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the US would be open to a diplomatic solution.
Iran’s supreme leader on Oct 31 warned the US and Israel against launching a new offensive, following threats that they could resume strikes after crucial elections in both countries.
Trump had previously warned an attack could come after the US midterms this week, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke of a “historic, one-time opportunity” to topple the Iranian government.
The elections in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict, with Israel having voted in a general election on Oct 27 but yet to form a new government.
“Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response,” Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told top military commanders, according to a statement.
Khamenei also ordered commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.
This was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and the military’s top brass.
He has not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March, after the killing of his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in US-Israeli strikes.
Rubio warned that “we can achieve military objectives if we seek to”, adding that Trump had not made a decision on any fresh strikes.
Oil price spike
Since the recent outbreak of the war, Tehran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.
Iran has previously warned that it would also consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
A ship traversing the strait struck a mine and caught fire, Iranian state television reported on Oct 31.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Oct 30 that three oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified “incidents” or hitting mines.
The blockade has caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the US public ahead of the upcoming polls.
Gains for the opposition Democrats could restrict, to an extent, Trump’s ability to enact policy.
Voting in Israel has left Netanyahu’s political camp with the most seats in Parliament but short of a majority, leaving the make-up of the next administration unclear.
‘Flames of war’
Fresh diplomatic efforts are under way to avert any resumption of fighting.
Qatari mediators landed in Tehran on Oct 30, and US Vice-President J.D. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
“I read the letter,” said Rezaei, in a video broadcast on Iranian television. “I haven’t yet responded. Their tone has completely changed,” he added, describing that as “a good sign”, without going into more detail.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were currently no plans for meetings with US officials.
“Iran’s conditions are clear and consultations regarding them are ongoing among mediators,” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Rezaei insisted Iran would continue to blockade the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions, including releasing frozen assets, were met.
Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks have yet to produce a lasting agreement.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.
“The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area,” he said on social media.
Araghchi warned on X that there would no longer be any “red lines”. AFP

articles.title: UK flies Protector drone on first home operation against Russian frigate
articles.body:
- An RAF Protector RG1 flew its first operational sorties in UK airspace, providing more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel.
- The aircraft supported HMS Dauntless and HMS Tyne as they tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14.
An RAF Protector RG1 remotely piloted aircraft has flown its first operational missions in UK airspace, giving the Royal Navy more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel while warships tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy, the UK Ministry of Defence said.
The unarmed Protector flew alongside military and civilian air traffic while the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless (D33) and offshore patrol vessel HMS Tyne (P281) monitored Neustrashimy and accompanying merchant ships through the Channel between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14. The ministry did not say how many sorties the aircraft flew, which sensors it used or how much of the frigate’s transit it covered.
“Protector’s first operational sorties in UK airspace demonstrate the significant value this capability brings to UK Defence. Working alongside Royal Navy vessels, it provided persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage, highlighting its ability to operate seamlessly across military and civilian airspace in support of maritime security, NATO commitments and wider UK tasking,” said Wing Commander Sam Haley, officer commanding XIII Squadron.
Protector is the RAF’s version of General Atomics’ MQ-9B SkyGuardian, flown from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire by 31 and XIII squadrons. The UK Military Aviation Authority issued it a military type certificate on April 29, 2025, clearing it to fly without geographic restrictions in UK airspace, and it entered service in June 2025 as the first remotely piloted aircraft authorized to do so. The MQ-9A Reaper it replaced never flew in UK airspace during its RAF career. The first of 16 Protectors arrived at RAF Waddington in 2023.
The RAF lists the aircraft’s endurance at more than 30 hours and its ceiling at up to 40,000 feet (12,200 m), with full-motion video, infrared imagery, synthetic aperture radar and ground target tracking among its sensors. In June 2026, a Protector flew from Waddington to RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus through European civil airspace, covering more than 2,000 nautical miles in about 13.5 hours.
The Channel mission was one of several Royal Navy operations against Russian ships between late September and mid-October. Merlin helicopters from Royal Naval Air Station Culdrose deployed to Glasgow Prestwick Airport under Operation Iceblast, a test of how quickly the Merlin force can operate away from its home base. From Sept. 29 to Oct. 8, they tracked the Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship Viktor Leonov near the Outer Hebrides, where NATO’s Exercise Strike Warrior was underway with more than 2,000 personnel from six nations.
From Oct. 11 to Oct. 14, HMS Tyne and a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron followed the Ropucha-class landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin, the cargo ship MV Energy-2 and the tug Proton through the Channel as they headed for the Baltic.
“HMS Dauntless monitored the movements of RFN Neustrashimy during her transit through the English Channel, contributing to the wider maritime picture and supporting UK maritime security,” said Commander Neil Skinner, commanding officer of HMS Dauntless.
Royal Navy activity monitoring Russian movements rose 25% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, the ministry said. Most of that work falls to patrol ships, frigates and helicopters; in January, HMS Mersey, HMS Severn and a Wildcat shadowed a Russian corvette and tanker through the same waters in a two-day operation coordinated with NATO allies.
“For the first time, Protector has joined Royal Navy warships and helicopters monitoring activity around our shores, demonstrating how we are constantly innovating to monitor and deter threats and irresponsible provocation,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
The ministry tied the operations to £298 billion (about $399 billion) in planned defense spending over the next four years and a commitment to reach 3% of GDP on defense in 2030. It also pointed to £330 million (about $442 million) over four years to protect undersea infrastructure and to Atlantic Bastion, a Royal Navy effort combining warships, patrol aircraft and autonomous systems against Russian submarines in the North Atlantic.

articles.title: Investors take out $3.6bn from Binance after record hack that stole billions
articles.body:
Investors have pulled $3.6bn (£2.7bn) in funds from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance as it recovers from a record hack in which billions were stolen from customer accounts.
The platform was hit by a $6.3bn theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history. Experts identified North Korea as the probable culprit.
Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach but on Sunday announced it had begun a phased reopening.
By Sunday afternoon, the platform had processed $4.6bn in withdrawals and $1bn in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of about $3.6bn – representing 2.1% of its $171bn in total assets under management.
The numbers were confirmed by the company in its latest proof of reserves snapshot. A full report is expected on Monday.
Binance said: “After an initial spike, withdrawal volumes have declined and are stabilising as expected, while deposit volumes have remained substantial.”
The crypto exchange told its customers that market conditions were stable and that its team was “testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets”.
“We know how important safe and reliable access to your funds is and will share details of the next phase as soon as we can,” it said on X.
In the first phase Binance restored withdrawals for 15 networks and assets, including ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain. Later on Sunday, dealing in the Dogecoin and Avalanche currencies resumed on their own platforms.
The platform said it had replenished 90% of the amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens were less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday.
Richard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the remaining 10%” and users would not bear the financial impact of the hack.
On Saturday the FBI confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said.
The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”.
Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
Binance said it had set aside about $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.
The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn secure asset fund for users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its futures insurance fund and own corporate treasury, Binance said on X.
The hack came as many observers expressed worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.

articles.title: The tactics of fighting in gas pipelines: why it matters in the Russian-Ukrainian war
articles.body:
The tactics of fighting in gas pipelines: why it matters in the Russian-Ukrainian war
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian and Russian troops move through gas pipelines, avoiding drones and launching surprise attacks on the enemy’s rear.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces have adopted the Russians’ tactic of fighting in underground tunnels. Military personnel from both warring countries are covering considerable distances through gas pipelines, trying to avoid the threat of drone strikes and catch the enemy by surprise. This is reported in an article by The New York Times, UNN reports.
Details
According to Maria Varenikova, a correspondent for The New York Times, while heading toward the entrance to the tunnel network, she narrowly escaped being hit by a Russian drone. She, the publication’s photographer, and the Ukrainian soldiers accompanying them had to jump out of the pickup truck on the move and hide from the Russian UAV along the road.
At the same time, journalist Simon Shuster notes in a publication on The Atlantic’s website that the new tactical methods are important for the course of the war. He discussed the issue with Ihor Obolenskyi, commander of the 2nd “Khartia” Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine.
The brigadier general said that initially, the Defense Forces tried to find the points where the Russians emerged onto the surface and destroy them. But they continued to appear several kilometers behind Ukrainian positions and attack.
The “Khartia” commander then turned to the state energy company with a request to provide maps of the pipeline network. The documents revealed the scale of the danger: it was a labyrinth of at least 57 steel pipes running beneath the combat zone, most of them one to two meters in diameter.
Previously, these pipes were used to pump Russian gas through Ukraine to European countries. But this stopped in 2025.
That same year, the Russians carried out “Operation Pipe”: between one hundred and several hundred soldiers crawled several kilometers along a section of the Urengoy–Pomary–Uzhhorod main gas pipeline and emerged behind Ukrainian troops in the Kursk region.
According to Obolenskyi, in October, after approximately six months of underground fighting, “Khartia” regained control of approximately 14 kilometers of pipelines in northeastern Ukraine as part of an operation codenamed “Veles.”

articles.title: Foreign media on Kazakhstan: Nuclear power, landmark Türkiye visit and major construction plans
articles.body:
Foreign media on Kazakhstan: Nuclear power, landmark Türkiye visit and major construction plans
As President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants, receives a ceremonial welcome from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and proposes declaring 2027 “the Year of Large-scale Construction” to develop public infrastructure nationwide, Qazinform News Agency presents its weekly review of Kazakhstan coverage in foreign media.
Euronews: Kazakhstan's Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a national uranium reserve and faster construction of two nuclear power plants in his annual state-of-the-nation address, Euronews reports.
“I believe it is possible, and perhaps even necessary, to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP as early as next year,” he said, also urging an agreement to advance the Moyynkum project.
Tokayev described an electricity surplus as essential for digitalization and artificial intelligence, while criticizing costly winter electricity imports followed by cheap summer exports.
He also urged Kazakhstan to capitalize on growing demand for overland transport.
“Kazakhstan must seize this historic opportunity to truly become a leading logistics hub for Eurasia,” he said.
The Aral-Caspian Highway is expected to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by 1,000 kilometres, while the Bakty-Ayagoz railway will add a third crossing with China.
Tokayev designated next year as the Year of Nationwide Construction, prioritizing public infrastructure.
Milliyet: President Erdoğan welcomed President Tokayev of Kazakhstan with an official ceremony
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan welcomed Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev with an official ceremony at the Presidential Complex in Ankara before bilateral and delegation-level talks, Milliyet reports.
The ceremony included both countries’ national anthems and a 21-gun salute. Tokayev greeted the guard of honor with “Hello, soldiers.”
According to Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications, the leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional and global issues.
Erdoğan said the two countries would strengthen their enhanced strategic partnership through further cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and the defense industry.
He also pledged close coordination with Kazakhstan during Türkiye’s chairmanship of the Organization of Turkic States.
Erdoğan invited Tokayev to attend the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya and was scheduled to host an official dinner in his honor.
Anadolu Agency: Türkiye, Kazakhstan to deepen defense industry cooperation
According to Anadolu Agency, Türkiye will deepen defense industry cooperation with Kazakhstan through joint production and mutually beneficial partnerships, Turkish defense industry chief Haluk Gorgun said on Wednesday.
His remarks followed talks in Ankara, where President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
Gorgun described Türkiye as a reliable, long-term partner offering competitive defense products and policies supporting joint production.
"We will diversify and deepen our areas of cooperation with friendly and brotherly Kazakhstan within the framework of a win-win approach," he said.
He added that combining the two countries’ expertise would contribute to the security and prosperity of the Turkic world.
Hürriyet: Turkic world leaders gather in Ankara for landmark summit
Ankara is hosting the 13th Organization of Turkic States summit on October 29-30 as Türkiye celebrates the republic’s 103rd anniversary, Hürriyet reports.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev was the first leader to arrive, receiving a ceremonial welcome from President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan before bilateral talks.
Held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Action,” the summit will address trade, energy, defense and transport, particularly the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor linking Asia and Europe.
Türkiye will assume the organization’s rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan. Leaders are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, appoint a new secretary-general and agree on measures to strengthen cooperation.
Commonspace.eu: Kazakhstan set for major construction program after Tokayev’s speech
According to Commonspace.eu, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed declaring 2027 “the Year of Large-scale Construction”, calling for new and renovated public infrastructure nationwide.
Priorities include roads, airports, railway stations, housing and healthcare facilities, alongside rehabilitation centers for children with special needs.
Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said the “People’s Construction” programme would drive infrastructure development and economic reforms.
“This large-scale project will provide significant momentum for employment growth and improving citizens’ well-being,” he said.
Healthcare Minister Akmaral Alnazarova outlined plans for nearly 70 healthcare facilities, including perinatal centers, children’s hospitals and rehabilitation branches. The projects would add or modernize 9,200 hospital beds.
Euronews: Gold market and central banks: Russia and Kazakhstan sell as Poland and China buy
Kazakhstan plans to reduce gold’s share of its reserves from around 78% to 75% by year-end, after ranking among the world’s biggest buyers in the first eight months of 2026, Euronews reports.

articles.title: From fridges to nuclear power plants, hackers are gaining control
articles.body:
In an unstable world super-charged by AI, hacking is the new war front
In the year 2000, on the sleepy banks of the Maroochy River on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, a new water treatment facility was experiencing technical difficulties.
Radio communications to wastewater pumps were not working, and the alarms designed to alert staff were not sounding.
Over a three-month period, more than 800,000 litres of untreated sewage was released into local waterways.
At first, council staff attributed the pump malfunctions to growing pains at the new plant.
But the real culprit? A hacker.
In the same year Australia cemented itself on the global stage hosting the first Olympics of the new millennia, it also secured its spot in the world of cybersecurity as the home of the first attributable case of operational technology hacking, becoming a case study used by engineers, academics and governments to this day.
Cyber-retribution a new war front
Operational technology (OT) is the hardware and software that monitors and controls physical machines.
OT is everywhere and is used to operate critical infrastructure such as power plants, conveyor belts, traffic lights, air traffic control systems and water treatment plants.
The Maroochy incident was 26 years ago, but OT hacking is now on the rise and will likely be supercharged by AI.
Last month, hackers remotely raised fridge and freezer temperatures across hundreds of French supermarkets.
In July, 30 water systems across the United States were attacked, consistent with methods used by an Iranian-backed hacking group the CyberAv3ngers.
In June, a cyber security incident brought Australia's second-largest raw sugar producer to a halt, shutting down milling and cane haulage. A Russian-speaking group called The Gentleman claimed responsibility.
In March, the Handala Hack group, also said to be operating under the Iranian government, claimed responsibility for cyber attacks against medical equipment supplier Stryker.
Since US President Donald Trump launched the war in Iran, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued warnings regarding "ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber targeting".
In other words: cyber-retribution.
Hacking has become targeted, a new war front for enemies across the globe to attack each other.
The Stryker hack was in retribution for the bombing of an elementary school in southern Iran.
Although the hackers targeted a US company, the attack put Australian hospitals on alert because it remotely wiped associated devices around the world.
Such attacks have obvious financial impacts, but as the technology powering them becomes more sophisticated, the scope and severity of the risks increase.
And as the world destabilises, incentives for hackers to cause harm, including the risk to human life, also increases.
Hacking goes nuclear
In 2025, hackers sponsored by China breached more than 400 agencies across the globe via Microsoft's SharePoint.
One of the agencies was the US National Nuclear Security Administration, the organisation responsible for managing the United States's nuclear stockpile, as well as the nuclear power plants on warships and submarines.
Although an IT hack, not an OT attack, Raji Rajagopalan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, explained that such breaches could be used to conduct an OT hack later.
"They get into a system, lie dormant for a very long time and when there is an opportunity, get into sensitive areas," Dr Rajagopalan said.
"That could create lots of different nuclear incidents that could be really disastrous from a humanitarian perspective."
One protection that nuclear facilities use to prevent such a disaster is an air gap, meaning that administrative systems are largely disconnected from operating systems.
However, Dr Rajagopalan said the assumption that these separations were watertight was not entirely true.
"There are digital upgrades, remote monitoring. All of these always compromise that air gap," she said.
A hacker remotely triggering a nuclear meltdown may sound like the work of Hollywood, but one known incident proved it is closer to reality than fiction.
Stuxnet is a highly sophisticated computer worm.
It was designed as part of Operation Olympic Games, a secret US-Israeli joint cyber-sabotage campaign — although the US government has never publicly taken responsibility.
Stuxnet was unleashed on the Natanz Iranian nuclear facility, where it lay undetected between 2009-2010.
The worm targeted the centrifuges used to enrich uranium, causing them to spin out of control until they broke. It was also sophisticated enough to hide what it was doing.
Stuxnet destroyed at least 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz and set Iran's nuclear program back by about a year.
Such attacks make global headlines when they are discovered, causing policymakers to make sweeping statements at press conferences.
But, Dr Rajagopalan said, political momentum was often lost after the fact.
"Somehow it seems all very theoretical, sounds very futuristic,"
she said.
"You don't want to scare people away, but at the same time, people need to understand that there are consequences to these attacks, that these attacks are real."
Critical infrastructure a sitting duck
Why is OT so vulnerable? How is it that the most critical infrastructure in the world is so at risk of being hacked?
UQ cyber security expert Ryan Ko said the main issue with OT was that much of it had been installed 20 to 30 years ago before existing knowledge of the latest cyber threats.
The old legacy systems were increasingly connected to the internet, he said, and every piece of critical infrastructure connected with OT was at risk.
And with the rise of AI, the scope of cyber-attacks had "changed drastically".
"It is now easier for an adversary to automatically detect a previously unknown vulnerability," Professor Ko said.
OpenAI's rogue agent Medicare data portal hack raised significant alarms for the Australian government.
Although not an OT attack, the incident highlighted how AI can efficiently find weaknesses that in other circumstances could be leveraged by bad faith actors.
Domestically, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) provides frameworks for governments and businesses to boost their cyber-defences against what it has described as "increasingly complex and persistent threats".
"Critical infrastructure and operational technology are attractive targets for state-sponsored cyber actors, cyber criminals and hacktivists," an ASD spokesperson said.
Can we stop OT spiralling out of control?
Dr Rajagopalan said as OT hacking incidents increased, the possibility of inadvertent incidents spiralling out of control also increased.
It is a scenario where neither side may want to engage in "big open-ended conflict, but things going out of control".
In a fracturing world, not only does the current geopolitical climate increase the incentive for enemies to attack one other, but it also limits the ability for allies to work with each other.
"We don't see the major powers coming together, discussing and debating these issues in full earnest,"
she said.
One solution for Australia, Dr Rajagopalan said, could be partnering with multilateral organisations such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations over major powers.
"Bring together smaller groupings of countries who have similar or like-minded interests and who have a certain amount of appeal to international law," she said.

articles.title: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces claim to have thwarted advancing Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces claim to have thwarted advancing Houthis
Yemen has claimed its army has been able to stop an advance by Houthi militants in the southwest of the country.
The hostilities between Yemen and its coalition allies and the Iranian-backed Ansar Allah movement escalated in September when the Shiite group seized the strategically important Red Sea port cities of Mocha and Dhubab as well as Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have since also encircled the country’s third-largest city, Taiz, with forces loyal to the internationally recognized government trapped inside.
According to Asharq Al-Awsat newspaper, which allegedly has close ties to the Saudi royal family, the Houthis mounted an offensive along the border between Lahij and Taiz governorates on Friday.
However, Saudi-backed troops reportedly pushed back the advancing militants, with airstrikes and artillery fire disrupting the Houthis’ supply lines, and staged a counteroffensive.
Fighting has also continued around the besieged city of Taiz.
Conflicting reports have been coming in regarding the situation in the north of Yemen over the weekend.
On Saturday, the internationally recognized government announced that its troops had recaptured positions in the northern governorate of al-Jawf, which borders Saudi Arabia. The Houthis, in turn, said that they had thwarted advances in the same governorate, as well as in neighboring Marib.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for multiple missile and drone strikes targeting strategic facilities in Saudi Arabia, including the Ras Tanura oil refinery, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, as well as a military installation in Najran region.
In a statement posted on X last Saturday, the Shiite group’s spokesman, Yahya Saree, stressed that the Houthis were conducting such attacks in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen.
Ansar Allah’s representative warned that strikes on Saudi territory would continue until Riyadh ended its “aggression” and lifted a blockade it had imposed on the neighboring country.
After the Houthis seized large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, government troops mounted a counteroffensive, claiming to have recaptured key positions near the vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Meanwhile, Riyadh has stepped up its air support, intensifying strikes on Houthi-held territory.
Yemen has remained locked in a civil war since 2014, with the situation further aggravated by a Saudi-led intervention launched the following year. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but flared up again in July after Saudi-backed government forces struck the Houthi-held Sanaa Airport.

articles.title: UK Intelligence Agency GCHQ Loses “Thousands” of Data Storage Devices
articles.body:
The UK’s Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), which is responsible for signals intelligence, cybersecurity, and protecting government and military information, has lost thousands of data storage devices containing sensitive information.
The Register reported this.
According to the annual report by the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office (IPCO), officials have known about the missing devices for years but still cannot determine exactly how many are missing.
The report describes the number as “very significant,” while GCHQ estimates that the maximum number of potentially missing devices is in the “thousands.”
“I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago,” investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson wrote.
The agency has launched a “program of further work” to recover as many missing devices as possible. This includes introducing an automated equipment-tracking system by year-end. According to GCHQ, once the system is operational, it will be able to determine the number of missing devices more accurately.
A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register: “As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to track the items that were registered for use effectively. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations.”
The missing storage devices are just one of the agency’s shortcomings highlighted in the IPCO report. The office also expressed “serious concerns” about inadequate safeguards intended to restrict UK foreign partners’ access to intercepted data collected by GCHQ.
GCHQ also came under scrutiny after a software bug in a web application used by “a relatively small proportion of the population” led to people being incorrectly identified as potentially involved in terrorist activity.
GCHQ is the UK’s signals intelligence (SIGINT) agency, responsible for cybersecurity and protecting government and military information. Together with MI5, which handles domestic security and counterintelligence, and MI6, the foreign intelligence service, it forms the country’s three main intelligence agencies.
In March 2025, a football fan found piles of classified military documents scattered along a street in northern England.
Some of the documents were marked “OFFICIAL – SENSITIVE.” They had fallen out of a black bin bag and were scattered across the road. They contained military ranks, email addresses, shift schedules, weapons-issue records, and information that appeared to relate to access to an arms storage facility and an intrusion detection system at Catterick Garrison.

Major fire breaks out at Kstovo oil refinery in Russia after drone attack
Drones have attacked the Kstovo oil refinery in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, causing a fire.
Source: Exilenova+ Telegram channel; Russian media outlet ASTRA; Supernova+ Telegram channel
Details: Footage showing a large fire in Kstovo began circulating on social media at around 04:11 this morning. Local residents reported explosions in the city, while monitoring Telegram channels said the Kstovo oil refinery had come under attack, with a major fire breaking out at several locations across the facility.
According to monitoring channels, the drones managed to strike the refinery despite Russian air defence forces having previously repelled attempts to attack the facility.
There have been no official comments from the local authorities so far. It is also unknown what weapons were used in the attack.
In addition, Exilenova+ reported a possible attack on the Novogorkovskaya combined heat and power plant, which is also located in Kstovo. It supplies energy to local industry, including petrochemical facilities. However, reports that it was hit require separate confirmation.
For reference: The Kstovo oil refinery is one of Russia's largest oil refineries. Its design capacity is around 17 million tonnes of oil per year. By this measure, it ranks fourth among Russian refineries, while it ranks second in terms of motor petrol production.

articles.title: Leader's advisor stresses shift in Iran's retaliation for war
articles.body:
In a Sunday post on his X account, Mohammad Mokhber said Iran is “rapidly” changing its military deterrence strategies to enable it to strike targets far beyond the West Asia region in response to a potential new act of aggression, Press TV reported.
“Of course, the geography of the threat no longer determines the geography of the response,” Mokhber said in the Farsi-language post.
“The redefinition of the scope of deterrence has gone beyond the regional framework, and the origin, scale, and location of a threat no longer impose any limits on Iran’s deterrence calculations,” he said.
The post comes amid concerns that Iran could face a new act of aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime, more than eight months after the two attacked the country without provocation.
Iran responded forcefully to the aggression by attacking targets deep inside the Israeli-occupied Palestinian territories, as well as military bases and assets controlled by the US in regional countries.
The extensive Iranian retaliation forced the US and Israel to end their 39-day aggression in mid-April under a ceasefire brokered by regional countries.
Iran has indicated that it will respond decisively to any new aggression, with military and security officials warning that the scope and scale of its counterattacks will be much greater this time.
On Saturday, Ayatollah Khamenei directed Iran's top military brass to prepare to deliver a swift and powerful response to any threat "without any geographic limitations."
Meanwhile, regional mediators have been trying to work out a diplomatic solution to the Iranian-US standoff, which has disrupted international energy and commodity supply chains.
Iran has indicated that it remains open to such a diplomatic solution if the US accepts its conditions for permanently ending the aggression and lifting its blockades and sanctions against the country.

articles.title: India trying to bring Russia, Ukraine & Europe to the table on 3 fronts: Jaishankar
articles.body:
India's External affairs minister S Jaishankar has discussed the protection of civilian shipping with Russia, Ukraine, and European nations
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said India has held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on protecting civilian shipping, restoring grain exports through the Black Sea and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.According to news agency ANI, Speaking on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said India was engaging with the parties on three key aspects of the conflict, including the safety of civilian vessels and seafarers, the restoration of grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine, and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure. He said India was trying to bring the concerned parties together to address these issues."One, not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers," he said, outlining the first of the three areas discussed with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
On the second issue, Jaishankar stressed the need to restore grain shipments from both Russia and Ukraine, warning that exports through the Black Sea had declined sharply amid the conflict."The second, to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine, these are two major exporters of grain for the global markets, can be restored, because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said.
Jaishankar further highlighted the complexities involved in ensuring the safety of energy infrastructure, saying different parties had different interpretations of what should be covered under such an understanding."And the third is with regard to energy. Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players. There is energy infrastructure itself. To some, it would mean a refinery; to some, it would mean grids. There would be issues relating to ships carrying fuel," he said.He added that India is attempting to bring the concerned parties together to find common ground on these issues, particularly on the protection of energy infrastructure and fuel shipments.
The concerns raised by Jaishankar extend beyond the immediate conflict, given the Black Sea's importance to global trade. Any disruption to commercial shipping can affect the movement of essential commodities, raise freight and insurance costs and put pressure on international supply chains.Similarly, attacks on refineries, electricity grids and fuel-carrying vessels can disrupt energy supplies and push up global prices. Together, the safety of maritime routes, grain exports and energy infrastructure remains critical to maintaining stability in global food and energy markets.
Aryan Singh is a journalist with The Times of India, covering breaking news, defence and global conflicts. An alumnus of the IIMC, he tracks the people, weapons and geopolitics behind the headlines, with a focus on India’s national security, military affairs and conflicts shaping the world.

articles.title: Jordan and Syria tout close ties, but border smuggling and strikes tell another story – analysis
articles.body:
Over the past week, tensions between Jordan and Syria appear to have increased in the wake of an attack on a church in Karak and a Jordanian airstrike on a terror cell in southern Syria. Southern Syria borders both Jordan and Israel’s Golan. Israel has been carrying out raids into Syria since the fall of the Assad regime. What might come next?
Additionally, Jordanian authorities “foiled an attempt to smuggle two million narcotic pills through the Jaber border crossing with Syria, the Public Security Directorate (PSD) said on Sunday,” Jordan Times noted. “The operation was carried out by Anti-Narcotics Department (AND) personnel at the border crossing in coordination with the Customs Department and other security agencies.” A PSD statement described authorities intercepting a suspicious cargo truck as it attempted to enter the country, following intelligence received about the vehicle.
The Jordanians found two million narcotic pills; this is not the first time. Jordan has been concerned about drug smuggling from Syria for years. During the reign of the Assads, the regime backed drug smuggling.
These days, the government in Syria does not support the smuggling, but the smugglers still exist. Some have said that smuggling routes stretch through and exploit the area of Sweida in southern Syria because of clashes between the Druze in Sweida and the government.
Meanwhile, Karaki police on Saturday seized nine automatic firearms and GPS devices after a suspicious bag was found in the Mochi area, according to PSD spokesperson Brig.-Gen. Amer Sartawi, Jordanian media said.
“Sartawi said that the bag had been carried by thermal balloons and preliminary investigations indicated that it had drifted with the wind from the kingdom’s southern border, adding that investigations are ongoing.”
This indicates that there are various security concerns across Jordan. In the past, there have been smuggling attempts from Jordan into Israel, which has increased its border security in the Jordan Valley in the last several years.
War and peace in Syria
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani said that Syria and Jordan maintain strategic relations and close security and military cooperation aimed at safeguarding their shared border and ensuring regional stability, Jordan media also noted. Shaibani made the comments at the 22nd Manama Dialogue events in Bahrain over the weekend.
Jordan Times noted that the top Syrian diplomat said, “The region faces growing challenges from cross-border militias and armed groups operating outside state institutions, undermining governments’ authority over decisions of war and peace.”
The diplomat added that “Syria has moved beyond the trenches of conflict to take its place in shaping regional security.” Shaibani visited southern Syria last week and made similar comments. He has argued that Syrian-Jordanian relations are “at their strongest in a century,” stressing that “the incident would not undermine ties between the neighboring countries.”
Shaibani added, “Jordan’s security is part of Syria’s security, and Syria’s security is part of Jordan’s security.”
A century of ties and tensions
Syria and Jordan share a long history shaped by the Arab Revolt, competing political ambitions, and recurring security crises. Their relationship dates back to the end of World War I, when the Hashemite-led Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire helped pave the way for Arab forces to enter Damascus in 1918.
Prince Faisal briefly ruled Syria before the French expelled him in 1920. His brother Abdullah subsequently established the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921. Faisal ended up ruling Iraq. The division of the region under British and French mandates left the two countries with close historical ties but different political trajectories.
Relations were frequently tense during the Cold War.
In September 1970, Syria sent armored forces into Jordan during the kingdom’s civil war, known as Black September, supporting the Palestinian terrorist groups that attacked King Hussein’s Jordanian forces. The intervention failed, but it left a lasting legacy of mistrust between Damascus and Amman.
At the time, Israel quietly backed Jordan. Jordan and Israel agreed to a peace deal in 1994.
Relations between Syria and Jordan improved periodically, particularly after Bashar al-Assad and King Abdullah II came to power.
The Syrian civil war, beginning in 2011, created new challenges. Jordan hosted hundreds of thousands of Syrian refugees and supported some opposition groups in southern Syria. However, Amman later sought to restore relations with Assad, reopening border trade and pursuing security cooperation.
Drug trafficking, particularly smuggling of the synthetic stimulant Captagon, remained a major concern, along with Iranian-backed militias operating in southern Syria.
Following Assad’s fall in 2024, Jordan moved to engage Syria’s new government under President Ahmad al-Sharaa.
Nevertheless, instability in Daraa and Sweida, cross-border smuggling, and the threat of armed groups continue to complicate relations. For Jordan, the priority remains a stable Syrian neighbor that can secure its borders and prevent regional conflicts from spilling into the kingdom.

articles.title: Thousands of Indians protest voter list change
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of Indians yesterday joined a protest led by opposition politicians in New Delhi, renewing demands for the country’s election chief to resign over an overhaul of voter lists they say unfairly benefits the ruling party.
The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests over the past month.
The Indian Election Commission said the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter lists, but the opposition said it is being manipulated to favor Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Photo: Reuters
The BJP and the commission deny the allegations.
Protesters led by opposition Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi chanted “vote thief, leave your seat” and beat drums while marching from central parts of New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue.
Gandhi said protesters were “not prepared to accept” the voter list removals.
“It is the theft of the voice of every single citizen of India,” he said. “This protest does not belong to any political party. It is India’s protest to save the democracy and constitution.”
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the opposition campaign.
The overhaul of India’s voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics said the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Members of the BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighboring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.
Election authorities said the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries, and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll.
Minister of Health and Family Welfare and senior BJP leader Jagat Prakash Nadda called the rally “a meticulously planned drama by those who have been defeated and repeatedly rejected by the people.”
“It is a calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy,” he said.
Protester Jayshree Roy said the government would have to listen if people “keep asking for their rights.”
“We have to keep showing up in large numbers, that is all that we can do,” the student said. “We have the power of people in our hands. That is all that we have.”

articles.title: Romania scrambles four fighter jets due to drone incursion
articles.body:
Romania scrambles four fighter jets due to drone incursion
Radar surveillance systems operated by Romania's Ministry of National Defence detected two unmanned aerial vehicles that had entered the country's airspace without authorisation on the evening of 31 October.
Source: Romania's Ministry of National Defence, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Romania scrambled four F-16 fighter jets and an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter to monitor the situation and manage the response after two unmanned aerial vehicles violated the country's airspace.
Alerts were issued in six Romanian counties due to the airspace violation: Iași, Neamț, Vaslui, Botoșani, Bacău and Suceava.
One of the two drones left the country's airspace, while the other was last spotted in the area between the counties of Vaslui and Bacău.
No drone crashes were reported.
Background:
- On the same day, a drone violated Moldovan airspace during Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine.
- On 23 October, Moldova's Foreign Ministry condemned the violation of the country's airspace by a drone and blamed Russia for the incident.
- After a drone was found in the village of Chiștelnița, just 100 m from a residential building, the ministry stated it would declare a Russian Embassy employee in Chișinău persona non grata.
- Romania is reportedly holding talks with Moldova on the joint development of counter-drone programmes.

articles.title: Russian drone strike near school dormitory kills 13-year-old in Vinnytsia Oblast, injures more children
articles.body:
First responders at the scene of a Russian strike on the territory of a vocational school dormitory on Nov. 1, 2026. (State Emergency Service/ Telegram)
A Russian drone strike on the grounds of a vocational school dormitory in Vinnytsia Oblast killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, on Nov. 1, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported.
Another six people were injured, including three 5-year-olds, a 16-year-old boy, and a 24-year-old man.
One of the injured five-year-olds is hospitalized in serious condition following the Russian attack that also set two cars ablaze before the fires were extinguished, Vinnytsia Oblast Governor Natalia Zabolotna said.
The dormitory damaged in the attack was currently being used to house internally displaced people escaping Russia's war, she added.
A car burns in the aftermath of a Russian strike on the territory of a vocational school dormitory on Nov. 1, 2026. (State Emergency Service/Telegram)
Photos shared by authorities also show first responders tending to a victim on a playground.
The Russian drone strike took place between the dormitory building and a school building in Vinnytsia Oblast's Kozyatyn district, Zabolotna said.
Russia regularly targets civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war.
On the morning of Oct. 29, Russian forces struck a train platform at Dnipro railway station, killing at least 15 people and wounding at least 14 more, authorities said.
"A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack. "The Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
Volodymyr Ivanyshyn is a news editor for The Kyiv Independent. He is pursuing an Honors Bachelor of Arts at the University of Toronto, majoring in political science with a minor in anthropology and human geography. Volodymyr holds a Certificate in Business Fundamentals from Rotman Commerce at the University of Toronto. He previously completed an internship with The Kyiv Independent.
A Russian drone strike on the grounds of a vocational school dormitory in Vinnytsia Oblast killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, on Nov. 1, the State Emergency Service reported.
"A ‘Pantsir-S2’ system and a command and control vehicle belonging to the S-400 ‘Triumph’ system were also struck," Zelensky said, causing an estimated $70 million in damage.
"The appointment of eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal lies within the constitutional power of the Sejm (Poland's parliament)," a European Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia continued its campaign against Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter, targeting infrastructure in at least four regions overnight and injuring three workers from the Ukrainian energy company DTEK.
Ukraine has targeted the facility a number of times, including a confirmed strike on Aug. 26 that sparked a large fire. The NORSI suspended operations due to damaged sustained in that attack.
"We're working to strengthen the protection of our people, our bilateral partnership with Turkey, and real diplomatic prospects. There are important issues concerning shipping in the Black Sea," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed uncertainty about whether a negotiated peace deal between Ukraine and Russia is possible, speaking at a G20 foreign ministers meeting on Oct. 31.

articles.title: Top Trump Officials Are Hitting the Campaign Trail Ahead of the Midterms. Are They Allowed To?
articles.body:
Top Trump Administration officials have taken to the campaign trail to boost Republican candidates ahead of the pivotal midterm elections as the party battles to retain control of Congress.
Last month alone, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum appeared alongside President Donald Trump to support Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in his tight reelection fight against Democrat Mary Peltola at a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appeared in Wisconsin alongside GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden on Oct. 20 to speak to manufacturing workers during a Pentagon tour highlighting U.S. defense production. Last Monday, Vice President JD Vance and Burgum spoke at a rally in Topeka, Kansas. And on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefly joined Trump on stage, at the President’s urging, during a rally in Corpus Christi, Texas.
Cabinet members and other leading Trump officials have been wading into the midterms in these and other ways for months. In August, for instance, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan.
Legal experts and advocacy groups contend that in making such moves, members of the Administration have violated a decades-old law: the Hatch Act, passed by Congress in 1939, which places restrictions on certain political activities for federal executive branch employees.
The Administration has argued that the officials have participated in political events in a strictly personal capacity, which is permitted under the Hatch Act, and that their actions have been cleared by lawyers and ethics officials.
But several top Trump aides—including at least nine of his 15 Cabinet secretaries—have been hit with formal complaints that their actions have violated the law.
“The number of Hatch Act violation complaints is extreme and abnormal for election time, especially for complaints against senior officials,” Kedric Payne, the head of ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, a legal non-profit that has filed a complaint against the Trump Administration for using taxpayer money to fund political ads, tells TIME.
“We are seeing with the Trump Administration why the Hatch Act is so important,” Payne says, “because when it is not enforced quickly, it can be abused.”
Here’s what to know about the Hatch Act, and the accusations that Trump officials have violated it.
What is the Hatch Act?
The Hatch Act is an 87-year-old federal law that prohibits certain government employees from using their “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election,” among other limits it imposes on officials’ political activity. It states that such interference applies to “an activity directed toward the success or failure of a political party” or candidate.
The law was established to ensure that “federal programs are administered in a nonpartisan fashion, to protect federal employees from political coercion in the workplace, and to ensure that federal employees are advanced based on merit and not based on political affiliation,” according to the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), which enforces it.
Many of the Hatch Act complaints against Trump officials on the campaign trail have centered around one specific aspect of the law that says federal employees cannot use or identify with their official title while engaging in political activity. In a handful of such complaints against members of the Administration, legal and press advocacy groups have pointed out that they were introduced at rallies by their Cabinet positions.
“Political activity must be conducted purely in your personal capacity, without using your official title, without implying endorsement of the United States government. In your personal time at your own personal expense,” Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W. Bush and a professor at the University of Minnesota law school, tells TIME.
The Trump Administration has pushed back on the accusations, saying that its members were acting in a personal capacity at the times in question.
How Trump Administration officials have been accused of violating the Hatch Act on the campaign trail
A number of complaints have been filed against the Trump Administration for violating the Hatch Act in recent months.
Two advocacy non-profits, The Democracy Defenders Fund and Reporters Without Borders, filed a complaint in October over the rally in Alaska that featured Trump, Lutnick, Burgum, and Carr. The groups claimed that Carr “impermissibly mixed his official work into his personal remarks” and requested that the OSC open an investigation into each Trump official’s conduct at the rally.
In September, the two advocacy groups also filed a complaint against Duffy for his appearance in Michigan and his endorsement of Rogers.
Chief Counsel at the Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement that Duffy’s conduct “crossed the legal and ethical line” and more broadly stated that it was “part of a broader pattern of this administration playing fast and loose with the law.”
Spokespeople for the Interior and Transportation departments have denied wrongdoing on the part of their respective leaders to media outlets. The FCC and Commerce Department did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment.
These complaints are among many more that have been filed over Administration officials’ participation in campaign activities.
“We haven't seen since the first Trump Administration this number of complaints against officials, and I've lost track, but I do think it's well over 20 complaints just in recent weeks,” Payne says.
In addition to complaints over officials’ appearances at campaign rallies, others have similarly alleged that Trump officials used their official titles in efforts to influence the midterms through social media and television network appearances.
CREW, a nonprofit government watchdog organization, has made several such claims. In one complaint from earlier this month, it argued that White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller violated the Hatch Act during an interview on Fox News in which he spoke against specific Democratic candidates running for office and urged voters to support a “pro-American Trump agenda.” The group has also filed complaints against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Kash Patel for comments made while speaking to Fox.
“These accusations are baseless and amount to a manufactured political attack," the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. "Secretary Kennedy takes his ethical obligations seriously, follows federal ethics laws, and consults HHS career ethics officials to ensure his activities comply with the standards governing public service.”
The Department of Department of Justice, which houses the FBI, did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment regarding the accusations against Patel.
When asked about the various Hatch Act complaints against Administration officials, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis tells TIME that “it has long been established that senior administration officials are allowed to discuss current events, policies, and the candidates involved with those policies in order to advance the agenda of the administration.”
Complaints allege further Hatch Act violations
Top Trump officials have additionally been accused of violating the Hatch Act through other means than direct statements and appearances in support of—or opposition to—midterm candidates that complaints allege may also affect the outcome of upcoming elections.
Payne and his colleagues filed a complaint accusing several Administration officials of using taxpayer money for political ads which the complaint describes as “touting partisan and political rhetoric” to influence the outcome of the midterms. The complaint cites three ads: one that promotes Trump’s actions in Iran, another that decries socialism, and a third that features Trump speaking at Mount Rushmore. The Campaign Legal Center in its complaint quotes parameters set by the OSC that say the Hatch Act is designed “to prevent the use of federal power and taxpayer resources to shape electoral outcomes and to preserve public confidence in the nonpartisan administration of the law.”
“Voters deserve to know that elected officials are campaigning using their own money and not taxpayer dollars,” Payne says. “Clearly these advertisements that were paid for by U.S. taxpayer dollars were intended to promote the Republican Party and influence the upcoming election.”
The complaint specifically requests an investigation into Trump officials including Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and White House Appointments Secretary Natalie Harp for their involvement in putting together the ads.
“There’s a statute that prohibits use of government funds for publicity or propaganda, unless expressly permitted by Congress,” Painter says. “Those ads that Trump was paying for with taxpayer dollars that said ‘paid for by the White House,’ that was propaganda. That violated that statute.”
Trump has defended the ads by saying he was “only promoting the country,” rather than specific candidates. “That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” he said when asked about the ads in the Oval Office in September.
A Hatch Act complaint was also filed against the Administration by the Democracy Defenders Fund over the raid federal agents conducted at Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Minnesota in October. The raid was reportedly part of an ongoing Department of Justice investigation into potential immigration fraud. Omar has denied all wrongdoing.
“The timing of this outrageous action against a long-time target of Trump’s evinces illegal political intent,” Norm Eisen, the co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “Staging a public raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress weeks before a consequential election is an abuse of power.”
Trump has maintained that he has “nothing to do” with the investigation, but has continued to levy public attacks against Omar, including calling her “crooked.”
The flurry of recent complaints against the Trump Administration are far from the first instances in which the President and his aides have come under fire for alleged Hatch Act violations.
An OSC report from 2021, for instance, found that in 2020, at least 13 senior Trump Administration officials violated the Hatch Act.
What is the penalty for a Hatch Act violation?
Following an investigation by the OSC, disciplinary measures for Hatch Act violations are determined by the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), an independent judicial agency within the Executive branch. For Cabinet or senior officials, OSC refers its findings to the President, who determines disciplinary action.
“The potential of those consequences happening under this President are small because it is up to the President usually to hold members of the administration accountable when they violate the Hatch Act,” Payne says, noting that in some cases, officials may be required to only issue a public apology for their violation, or face no consequence at all.
Federal officials who have previously been found to have violated the Hatch Act under Trump largely have not faced repercussions because the President either declined to punish them or because the OSC reported the violations after Trump and the officials in question left office.
After one OSC report from 2018 found Kellyanne Conway, a former counselor to Trump, had violated the Hatch Act, for example, Trump declined to fire her, telling Fox & Friends at the time that “it looks to me like they’re trying to take away her right of free speech and that’s just not fair.”
The OSC itself has meanwhile acknowledged that it was reporting other violations at a point when disciplinary action could not be taken. “Though discipline is no longer possible once subjects leave government service, OSC is issuing this report to fully document the violations, highlight the enforcement challenges that OSC confronted in investigating the violations, and to deter similar violations in the future,” one OSC report from 2021 reads.
Federal employees can face several civil penalties if they are found to have violated the Hatch Act, however, including a fine, a suspension, or a letter of reprimand. For a criminal violation, up to three years in prison may be imposed as a penalty if an official is found to have “intimidate[ed], threaten[ed], command[ed], or coerce[ed] … any employee of the Federal Government … to engage in, or not to engage in, any political activity.”
“If President Trump or anyone overreaches the point of trying to coerce someone in the government to engage in partisan conduct, that's a violation of the criminal provision of the act, but all the rest of it's civil,” Painter explains.
