articles.title: 'Some optimism' in US-Iran negotiations despite major disagreements, sources tell 'Post'
articles.body:
“Some progress” has been made in efforts to reach an agreement between the US and Iran, several sources familiar with the negotiations told The Jerusalem Post. However, the sources stressed that "significant gaps remain between the two sides".
“There is some optimism that an agreement can be reached. But there is still work to be done,” one source said.
Another source said no progress had been made on the nuclear issue and that the advances concerned other matters, including the timeline for implementing a potential agreement.
In recent days, Qatari mediators have intensified indirect diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran amid growing fears of a potential military escalation following the US midterm elections.
An Iranian delegation traveled to Doha for several days of talks, coordinated closely with Washington, following intensive consultations in Tehran. The discussions reportedly focus on proposals to de-escalate the eight-month-old conflict, including a potential two-day framework for reopening the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz and resuming broader peace negotiations.
Significant gaps remain over Iran's nuclear program
Despite these diplomatic efforts, significant gaps remain between the two sides. Tehran is demanding that Washington lift recent sanctions, reinstate oil waivers, reduce its regional military presence, and end port blockades before addressing restrictions on Iran's nuclear program.
By contrast, US officials, following recent outreach by Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei, insist that any comprehensive agreement must address nuclear concerns from the outset.
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump was asked how negotiations with Iran were progressing.
“They're going fine, but they're not very reliable. They make a deal and then they back out,” he responded.
Trump also said there were “one or two sites” in Iran's nuclear program that the US needed to address.
“But we can do that in 10 minutes,” he added.
A source familiar with the matter confirmed to the Post that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump spoke by phone on Saturday. The call came days after Trump was briefed by US Central Command (CENTCOM) commander Adm. Brad Cooper on military options for a possible operation against Iran.
Meanwhile, Iranian Deputy Parliament Speaker Ali Nikzad said Iran had no intention of negotiating over its nuclear program, regardless of the pressure exerted on it.
Can Washington and Tehran overcome the nuclear deadlock?
Dr. Raz Zimmt, head of the Iran and Shi'ite Axis Research Program at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Jerusalem Post that each side currently needs something from the other that cannot be reversed, while neither is willing to make what would constitute an irreversible concession.
“The Americans are prepared to lift the naval blockade and some of the sanctions, since these measures can be reinstated, and in return they are demanding something on the nuclear front, such as an inspectors' visit and/or action regarding the enriched uranium. The Iranians, meanwhile, are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and perhaps even allow inspectors to visit certain sites, but they are unwilling to give up their enriched uranium. Instead, they are demanding something permanent, such as the unfreezing of Iranian assets.
“I find it difficult to see how this deadlock can be resolved,” Zimmt said.
Nevertheless, he added that, given the risks of another round of military confrontation, he would not rule out the possibility that the two sides could ultimately reach a compromise, even if only a temporary one.

articles.title: Ukraine evacuates civilians from parts of Kherson region as expiry of Oleshky ceasefire nears
articles.body:
Ukraine evacuates civilians from parts of Kherson region as expiry of Oleshky ceasefire nears
Nov 1 - Ukraine's military said it evacuated 167 people from threatened areas of southern Kherson region on Sunday as a temporary local ceasefire neared expiry -- two days after busloads of residents were brought out of the embattled Russian-held town of Oleshky.
A six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo. The ceasefire was due to expire at midnight Moscow time (2100 GMT).
It is the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
"Units of civil-military cooperation of the 'South' group of forces, in cooperation with representatives of local authorities, evacuated 167 civilians to safer points in the Kherson region," Ukraine's General Staff wrote on Telegram.
It said the evacuees included 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility requiring special assistance.
The governor of Kherson region, Oleksandr Prokudin, urged residents to be vigilant as the expiry of the ceasefire neared.
"I also strongly urge you not to visit the so-called 'red zones' – areas and settlements near the Dnipro," Prokudin wrote on Telegram. "The intensity of Russian strikes there remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high."
In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said Russia had a positive view of how the operation was conducted in Oleshky, as well as of the coordination between the two countries' human rights commissioners.
The pope said he hoped cooperation between Russia and Ukraine in implementing a ceasefire in Oleshky would pave the way for broader peace efforts.
Melania Trump, writing on X, said the ceasefire "has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack".
On Saturday, starved and exhausted residents of Oleshky crossed into Ukraine after a circuitous journey from the area, just a few km (miles) from the front line.
They first travelled by bus via Crimea, annexed by Russia from Ukraine in 2014, to the Russian town of Anapa, before flying to Belarus from where they continued to Ukraine.
Those wishing to leave Oleshky - some for Russia, some for Ukraine - were taken initially to Crimea in 25 buses and nine ambulances, Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova said, before splitting into separate convoys.
It was not known how many chose to stay in Russian-held Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River opposite the region's Ukrainian-held main town of Kherson.
CEASEFIRE HOLDING
The ceasefire has been holding since Tuesday without violations, according to both Ukrainian and Russian officials. It has allowed them to de-mine the roads and bring food, medicines and other supplies into the town.
Russian forces took control of the town immediately after the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, but Ukrainian troops recaptured much of the region, including the town of Kherson, later that year.
Military action continued in other parts of Ukraine on Sunday.
Regional governors and emergency services reported one death in a strike in the Sumy region on the Russian border, a frequent target, and at least one in the central region of Vinnytsia. REUTERS

articles.title: Al Jazeera marks 30 years of transforming news in Middle East and beyond
articles.body:
Al Jazeera marks 30 years of transforming news in Middle East and beyond
The anniversary coincides with a significant restructuring of Al Jazeera Media Network’s Arabic-language news services.
Doha, Qatar – As Al Jazeera marks its 30th anniversary with a special commemorative event, the media network’s history is a timeline of milestones and challenges – from risks, obstacles and attacks, to international awards and recognition from the communities whose stories it strives to tell.
Launched on November 1, 1996, the network broke new ground in Arab broadcasting, bringing previously marginalised political perspectives into the mainstream and creating space for debate on issues seldom openly discussed on regional television.
On Sunday, the network hosted an event to commemorate its enduring legacy at its headquarters in the Qatari capital, Doha, attended by the Emir of Qatar Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and other delegates.
Since its launch, Al Jazeera was not “just a screen”, said Al Jazeera’s Director General Sheikh Nasser bin Faisal Al Thani at the anniversary event. “It was a promise that journalism can be free and responsible, and that ‘opinion and the other opinion’ is not just a slogan, but it’s a position you take.”
For three decades, Al Jazeera “has helped transform the way news is covered in the Arab world”, Director of News Raed Fakih said in a statement, hailing the network for making room for “voices, issues and perspectives that had not been given the space they deserved”.
“Today, as we mark Al Jazeera’s 30th anniversary, we are building on that editorial legacy to broaden the scope of our coverage and give greater prominence to a wider range of events and viewpoints,” he added.
The anniversary coincides with a significant restructuring of Al Jazeera Media Network’s Arabic-language news services, separating rolling breaking news coverage, live event broadcasting, and more in-depth reporting across three channels.
Risks, obstacles and attacks
Since Qatar’s late Father Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani launched the independent channel – a first in the Arab world – the network has promised to provide “the opinion and the other opinion”.
It launched its first TV broadcast as an Arabic-language satellite news channel in 1996 from Doha and has since then grown into the Al Jazeera Media Network, with several outlets in multiple languages. A private corporation for public benefit, the network now includes television channels, websites and other digital platforms.
But as governments have banned it, and as its offices have been bombed in many parts of the world, the network has exacted a huge cost for staying on air.
Yet it has been instrumental in covering key events in the last three decades in the region and beyond.
In 2001, when the United States attacked Afghanistan, Al Jazeera was the only foreign broadcaster in Kabul, its updates and pictures travelling the world.
Then in 2011, millions followed the Arab Spring uprising live on Al Jazeera. Its coverage won a prestigious Peabody Award.
However, the network’s reporting has led to numerous threats over the years. Exclusive pictures have made Al Jazeera hard to ignore, but have also made the network a target.
In 2003, a US strike hit its Baghdad office, killing correspondent Tareq Ayyoub. Two dozen Al Jazeera journalists have been killed since.
In 2022, an Israeli soldier shot Palestinian correspondent Shireen Abu Akleh in Jenin, the 12th Al Jazeera journalist killed in 19 years. Another 12 were then killed in just 30 months, every one of them by Israel during its genocidal war in Gaza.
One of them was Anas al-Sharif, who for many viewers was the face of the war. In August 2025, an Israeli strike killed him and four colleagues as it hit a press tent outside al-Shifa Hospital.
“To the martyrs of Al Jazeera, to our colleagues who departed while carrying out their duties, we say to them today, you are part and parcel of Al Jazeera’s promise,” Al Jazeera’s Sheikh Nasser said at the event on Sunday.
Meanwhile, across the region, governments have closed the network’s bureaus and pulled the channel’s licences.
In 2024, Israel banned the network and raided its Ramallah office. Months later, the Palestinian Authority suspended it.
Overall, at least nine governments have tried to silence Al Jazeera.
A new technological era
Despite the challenges, Al Jazeera’s broadcast continues, with more than 3,000 staff working out of more than 70 bureaus across the globe.
Alongside its digital divisions, as well as its English channel that launched in 2006, Al Jazeera reaches more than 430 million homes.
The network on Sunday also launched The Core, an artificial intelligence (AI) initiative first announced in December 2025 in collaboration with Google Cloud. The initiative aims to integrate AI into newsroom operations, helping journalists manage information, coordinate coverage and make better use of the network’s reporting archives.
Meanwhile, Al Jazeera Balkans was also relaunched in a new digital-first format, opening a new chapter in its journalism in the region.
While the network’s shelves are packed with hundreds of awards, it continues its mission of serving as a voice of the voiceless.

articles.title: Rubio doubts Ukraine peace deal can be reached any time soon – Radio Liberty
articles.body:
Rubio doubts Ukraine peace deal can be reached any time soon – Radio Liberty
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has privately told his Western counterparts that he is uncertain whether the war in Ukraine can be ended through negotiations or whether Kyiv will be able to join NATO in the near future.

articles.title: 'No military solutions': EAM Jaishankar reveals PM Modi-Putin talks on Ukraine conflict in Delhi, Bishkek
articles.body:
File photo: PM Modi with Russian President Vladimir Putin
NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar has said Prime Minister Narendra Modi discussed the Ukraine conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin in New Delhi and earlier in Bishkek, as India continues diplomatic engagement with Moscow, Kyiv and Washington on measures to protect civilian shipping, restore grain exports and safeguard energy infrastructure.Speaking exclusively to news agency ANI on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta on Saturday, Jaishankar said India had held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on three key aspects of the conflict."Prime Minister himself had a discussion with President Putin in Delhi and before that in Bishkek," he said, referring to India's diplomatic engagement.
Jaishankar said he had also discussed the conflict with Russian and Ukrainian officials, including during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, and in talks with Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov.
"We have also been coordinating this with the Americans because they have their own peace mediation initiative. So Secretary Rubio knows properly what is going on here," he said.
India focuses on civilian shipping, grain exports and energy security
Explaining the three areas under discussion, Jaishankar said India was first seeking to ensure that civilian vessels and seafarers were not targeted in the conflict.The second priority was to restore grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, both major suppliers to international markets.
He said shipments through the Black Sea had fallen sharply because of the conflict."One not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers. The second is to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine. Then these are two major exporters of grains for the global markets. Find a way of restoring that flow because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said.The third area concerned energy infrastructure and shipments. Jaishankar said this was the most complicated issue because the concerns differed among the parties involved."Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players," he said, referring to refineries, electricity grids and ships carrying fuel.He added that India was trying to bring the parties together to address these concerns but could not publicly disclose the current status of the discussions.
Jaishankar calls for diplomatic solutions to global conflicts
At the G20 meeting, the external affairs minister reiterated India's position that major international conflicts required diplomatic engagement rather than military escalation."Look, there are big conflicts today, two major conflicts which are having global ramifications," he said, adding that "there are no military solutions; we have to find a diplomatic pathway."Jaishankar also flagged the impact of disruptions in energy markets and fuel distribution on developing economies."This distortion of the energy markets, the politicisation of energy flows, this is something which is very harmful," he said, adding that the Global South was bearing the brunt of energy shortages.He also raised concerns over disruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea and fertiliser shortages linked to tensions along the Persian Gulf and Red Sea corridors.On supply chain resilience, which was the focus of the G20 meeting's concluding plenary session, Jaishankar called for greater diversification of global production and manufacturing networks."Today we need more diversified supply chains," he said, advocating "more globalised, you know, more diversified production, more diversified manufacturing."In a post on X after the session, he said securing resilient supply chains was central to the well-being of the global economy. He also called for promoting the "right to industrialise", resisting "predatory practices" and pursuing the "de-politicisation of markets".
Jaishankar meets Russian, Polish and South Korean counterparts
On the sidelines of the G20 meeting, Jaishankar held separate discussions with his Russian, Polish and South Korean counterparts on the Ukraine conflict, West Asia, bilateral ties and multilateral issues.After meeting Lavrov, Jaishankar said the two sides had discussed the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf situation and multilateral issues.He also met Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, with discussions focusing on the Ukraine conflict, India-European Union ties and the G20."My meeting with DPM & FM Radosław Sikorski @sikorskiradek of Poland focused on the Ukraine conflict, India-EU ties and the G20," Jaishankar said.Poland is participating in this year's G20 meetings as a full participant following an invitation from the United States. It has also expressed interest in securing permanent membership of the grouping.
Jaishankar separately met South Korean foreign minister Cho Hyun to review bilateral cooperation and discuss G20-related and other multilateral issues."Appreciated the stocktaking with @FMChoHyun of the Republic of Korea of our bilateral cooperation, as also the discussion on G20 and multilateral issues," he said.Earlier on Saturday, Jaishankar also participated in the Quad Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta with US secretary of state Marco Rubio, Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi and Australian foreign minister Penny Wong.The US is holding the G20 presidency this year. After two days of discussions, Jaishankar and other foreign ministers attended a college football game between the Florida Gators and the Georgia Bulldogs at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta.

articles.title: Ukraine claims strike on major Russian oil refinery near Moscow
articles.body:
Russia said on Sunday that a drone had struck an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight, after Ukraine claimed it had hit a major oil refinery.
Gleb Nikitin, governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, reported a "massive drone attack" during the night, during which an "industrial enterprise in the Kstovo district sustained significant damage".
"More than 100 drones destroyed," and "according to preliminary information, there are no casualties," he added in a statement, without specifying the plant's activities.
Ukrainian media reported an attack on the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it "one of Russia's largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants".

articles.title: U.S. Army’s HADES spy plane prototype makes first flight
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army’s HADES Prototype 1, a modified Bombardier Global 6500 jet, made its first flight on Sept. 11, the service announced Oct. 30.
- The aircraft now enters developmental flight testing of its multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence systems ahead of operational demonstrations.
The U.S. Army’s first HADES prototype, a Bombardier Global 6500 business jet modified by Sierra Nevada Corporation for long-range signals intelligence and deep sensing, made its first flight on Sept. 11, the service announced on Oct. 30, seven weeks after the event.
The flight followed a flight readiness review and moves the High Accuracy Detection and Exploitation System into mission system integration and a developmental flight test program. The Army said those tests will check the aircraft’s multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence equipment ahead of operational demonstrations. It did not say where the aircraft flew, how long the flight lasted or what mission equipment was installed.
“The first flight of HADES Prototype 1 transitions our vision for deep sensing from concept to reality,” said Lt. Col. (P) James Hickey, project manager for the Fixed Wing Project Office. “This achievement reflects the dedication, technical precision, and shared mission focus of our military, civilian, and industry partners working to deliver transformational capabilities to the Army and joint force.”
The Fixed Wing Project Office ran the flight with SNC, the program’s lead systems integrator, and with the Project Director Sensors–Aerial Intelligence, part of the Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Command and Control/Counter-Command and Control. Before the flight, engineers, test pilots and mission system architects completed the structural modifications, installed mission system hardware and finished preliminary airworthiness checks. HADES is government-owned and contractor-operated, and SNC told Defense Daily in January that its own pilots and technicians would fly the tests alongside the Army.
Bombardier delivered the first Global 6500 for the program to the Army in Wichita, Kansas, in November 2024, and the Army passed it to SNC’s facility in Hagerstown, Maryland, for conversion. The Army had picked SNC as lead systems integrator in August 2024 under a 12-year contract worth $93.5 million at award, with a ceiling of $991.3 million, beating a team of L3Harris, Leidos and MAG Aerospace. L3Harris protested the decision, which stopped work until the Government Accountability Office denied the protest on Dec. 23, 2024. SNC received the second Army-owned jet in September 2025, and at the end of 2025 it bought a fourth Global 6500 with its own money to become the first non-prototype aircraft in the fleet.
The Army plans to field HADES in stages. In April 2026, Army officials said the program would deliver three prototypes, with the second adding an advanced radar and the third described as “combat credible”, and that the first aircraft would reach units later this year. The service also wants to pair HADES with launched effects, small unmanned systems released from the aircraft. In 2025, the Army said it would buy about half as many of the jets as it had previously planned, and it has not published a final fleet size.
When it announced the 2024 award, the Army said SNC would integrate communications intelligence, electronic intelligence, synthetic aperture radar and moving target indicator sensors on the Global 6500. A Pentagon budget reprogramming document approved in early 2025 confirmed that Raytheon’s Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar System-2B, developed for the U.S. Air Force’s U-2, is part of the HADES sensor suite. The Oct. 30 release mentions only multi-domain sensing and signals intelligence for the current test phase.
HADES grows out of a string of contractor-owned bridging aircraft the Army has flown since 2020. Leidos built ARTEMIS on a Bombardier Challenger 650 and ARES on a Global 6500, and ARES deployed to the Indo-Pacific in 2022. Under the follow-on ATHENA effort, a MAG Aerospace and L3Harris team modified Global 6500s for radar collection, while SNC converted two jets to its RAPCON-X signals intelligence configuration, which became the basis for HADES. SNC says the HADES aircraft will be the first Army-owned large-cabin business jets used for aerial intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.
The jets are meant to replace the Army’s legacy turboprop intelligence aircraft. The Army says the Global 6500 airframe offers greater speed, range, payload and operating altitude than those platforms, which lets HADES collect from farther away and spend more time on station in large-scale operations.
“Deep sensing is critical to maintaining decision advantage in the future fight,” Hickey said. “HADES will help commanders see farther, understand faster, and act with greater precision across the multi-domain battlefield.”

articles.title: Araghchi: Iran ready for both defense and diplomacy; Choice rests with US
articles.body:
Araghchi: Iran ready for both defense and diplomacy; choice rests with US
TEHRAN – Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to pursue diplomacy while maintaining full defensive preparedness, saying the next step depends on the United States and whether Washington chooses a rational diplomatic approach.
Speaking to ICANA, the Iranian Parliament’s news outlet, Araghchi discussed the recent visit by an Iranian delegation to Qatar and continued consultations with Qatari mediators.
He said the delegation, led by a deputy foreign minister, travelled to Doha to continue discussions with Qatari mediators, who had also visited Tehran in recent weeks.
Araghchi stressed that the visit was not intended to involve direct negotiations with the United States, adding that consultations with the mediators on a two-day proposal were still underway.
According to the Tehran Times, consultations with Qatari mediators were continuing over a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, provided that the United States met Iran's conditions. Under the proposal, the US would take the required steps on the first day, while the waterway would reopen on the second day, allowing maritime traffic to return to its previous state.
“Discussions on the two-day proposal are continuing, and the process is moving forward, but we have not yet reached a definitive outcome,” he said, noting that progress depended on the answers the other side provided to Iran’s questions.
The foreign minister said Tehran was making every effort to advance the diplomatic process and expressed hope that Washington would also demonstrate the necessary rationality to prioritize diplomacy over other options.
Turning to Iran’s defense preparedness, Araghchi referred to directives issued by the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces to senior military commanders, saying they clearly demonstrated the Islamic Republic’s resolve.
He added that Iran’s Armed Forces had been assigned a clear mission and had become stronger than before by drawing on the experience gained in the two previous wars.
Araghchi reiterated that Iran remained prepared for both defense and diplomacy, emphasizing that the course of future developments would depend on the decisions and judgment of the United States.
“Whether the Americans choose diplomacy or another path depends on their own rationality,” he said.

articles.title: Iranian tech firms showcase innovations at exhibitions in Russia, China

Iranian tech firms showcase innovations at exhibitions in Russia, China
TEHRAN – Iranian knowledge-based companies have participated in two major international exhibitions, Kazan Digital Week in Russia and Aquatech China, showcasing their technological capabilities and exploring opportunities to expand international cooperation and business ties.
With the support of the Innovation and Prosperity Fund, the representatives of nine Iranian knowledge-based firms paid a visit to the Kazan Digital Week Expo held from October 29 to 31, holding meetings with officials from the Tatarstan Investment Development Agency and representatives of Russian technology companies, IRNA reported.
Exploring joint investment opportunities, conducting business meetings with companies based at IT parks, and paying a visit to Innoploice urban settlement were among other plans of the delegation.
The expo primarily focused on developing a sustainable ecosystem of trusted digital technologies and the use of digital technologies in industries, businesses, and government.
The exhibition included scientific conferences, expert sessions, business meetings, start-up events, training workshops, and initiatives to foster international collaborations. It provided a great opportunity for showcasing the latest innovative technologies, developing export markets, attracting investment, and establishing strategic partnerships.
In October, leading Iranian and Russian companies explored ways to expand bilateral cooperation in advanced technologies at the third Russia-Iran Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Forum.
The forum brought together officials, diplomats, and public- and private-sector representatives from both countries. The participants met on the sidelines of the second Global Digital Forum, held in Moscow from October 8 to 10, IRNA reported.
During the meeting, Alexander Shoitov, Russia’s deputy minister of digital development, communications and mass media, said the participation of Iranian companies in the Global Digital Forum offered a valuable opportunity to exchange information and establish new partnerships.
He noted that Iran and Russia had significant potential to expand bilateral cooperation, particularly in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.
Shoitov also reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to deepen bilateral ties and develop joint infrastructure in the ICT sector.
For his part, Iran’s ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, highlighted the importance of fostering strategic cooperation between Iran and Russia in the expansion of digital exchanges within a governmental framework. The enhancement of ties helps strengthen the country’s capacity for participation in regional and global markets.
Highlighting the expertise and knowledge of Iranian technology companies in the localization of IT infrastructure equipment, Russian companies can establish joint ventures with reliable partners in Iran, gaining access to the country’s IT and artificial intelligence services market.
Moreover, Iranian and Russian representatives of high-technology companies showcased their latest cutting-edge accomplishments and presented their comprehensive plans and operational proposals for the promotion of cooperation in advanced technologies.
Exchanging best practices and technological solutions, holding B2B meetings, expanding business networks, and exploring opportunities for joint projects were among other key parts of the Forum.
Particular attention was given to practical mechanisms for Russian and Iranian companies to enter new markets and develop cooperation with partners from third countries.
Aquatech China
Also, a trade and technology delegation consisting of representatives of some 16 knowledge-based companies attended Aquatech China, with the aim of expediting the internalization and export of knowledge-based products. The exhibition was held in Shanghai from October 28 to 30.
The delegation paid a visit to different parts of the exhibition and held meetings with the participating companies.
Aquatech China is the leading water technology trade show in China, covering all aspects of water: drinking water, industrial water, wastewater treatment, sludge treatment, smart water solutions, and water management.
The increasing need for (clean) water, combined with promoting environmental protection and strong enforcement of new regulations, creates huge opportunities for international companies specialized in (waste)water technologies in China.
In August, the Iran National Science Foundation (INSF) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) announced support for the second joint specialized workshops to develop science diplomacy, foster research networking, and exchange technical knowledge.
The grant, amounting to 7 billion rials (about $2.6 million) per research project for one year, will be allocated to the following fields, IRNA reported.

Exploration and processing of rare earth elements
 
Nano-composites for resilient construction materials in earthquake-prone areas
 
Green synthesis of nanomaterials using biological resources
 
2. Novel Sensors:
 
Smart nanomaterials for biosensors: early detection of diseases and pathogens
 
Nanostructured gas sensors for environmental and industrial pollution monitoring
In July, the INSF and the NSFC announced support for the implementation of 15 research projects by faculty members. The grant, amounting to 50 billion rials (some $26,595) for each research project for at least three years, would be allocated to the following fields, INSF.org reported.
Water and Energy: AI-powered smart irrigation systems for water-scarce and saline environments; Integrated water resource management under drought and climate variability conditions; and Energy-efficient advanced technologies for water treatment and seawater/brackish water desalination.
Energy storage and hydrogen technologies: Renewable energy integration into national grid and distribution networks; Agricultural and medical biotechnology; Genetic improvement of strategic crops for drought, salinity and heat resistance using molecular breeding techniques; Microbial biotechnology for food security: bio-fertilizers, single-cell proteins, and probiotics, biopesticides and biological control; Recombinant drugs and biosimilars: process development, purification, and quality control; and Novel drug delivery systems based on biological origins (nano-carriers, liposomes).

Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook
Quote: "During the ceasefire imposed in designated areas of Kherson Oblast to carry out the humanitarian mission in Oleshky, Ukraine's defence forces used the opportunities created by the safety situation to evacuate residents from the right bank of Kherson Oblast.
The evacuation involved settlements in Ukrainian-controlled territory along the Dnipro River, which had been subjected to daily attacks by Russian forces. Those who had previously been unable to leave the dangerous areas were able to evacuate.
Units of the Civil-Military Cooperation Department of the Pivden (South) Group of Forces, working with representatives of local authorities, evacuated 167 civilians to safer locations in Kherson Oblast. They included 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility who required special attention and assistance."
Details: The General Staff noted that the evacuation took place in extremely difficult and dangerous conditions. The routes passed through mined and damaged roads, as well as areas where military equipment and civilian cars had been burnt out. All this significantly complicated movement and required particular caution and coordinated action by all units involved.
The General Staff stressed that units of the Pivden Group of Forces have been strictly and consistently observing the ceasefire in the area of the humanitarian mission.
Background:
- The White House announced that US First Lady Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, where a humanitarian disaster is currently unfolding.
- Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets announced that a ceasefire would come into effect at 03:00 on 27 October in the Oleshky area. Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed this. The ceasefire is due to continue until 22:59 on 1 November.
- Under the agreement between the Russian and Ukrainian sides, the evacuation route for Oleshky residents ran through Russia and Belarus to Ukraine. Lubinets' office explained why the evacuation would take place along this route. Some people evacuated to Ukraine, while others chose to go to Russian-controlled territory.
- On 31 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that the humanitarian operation in Oleshky had been successfully completed. All Ukrainian citizens evacuated crossed the state border in Chernihiv Oblast.

articles.title: Sudan accuses Ethiopia over drone attacks amid fresh strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Sudan accuses Ethiopia of enabling drone attacks as strikes hit northern power stations
Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used to launch drone attacks on civilians and vital infrastructure, as fresh strikes on two northern power stations on Sunday extended a wave of attacks disrupting electricity supplies across the country.
Foreign ministry undersecretary Muawiya Othman told a diplomatic briefing on Saturday that Ethiopia was participating in what he described as a proxy war on behalf of regional actors, particularly the United Arab Emirates, which Sudan’s army-aligned government accuses of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
He alleged that the Assosa base in western Ethiopia had become a hub for supplying the RSF with weapons and equipment and facilitating the movement of foreign fighters into Sudan. He described the alleged use of Ethiopian territory to launch drone strikes as the most dangerous aspect of that support.
Ethiopia denies the accusations and has countered that the Sudanese army is supporting rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an allegation Khartoum rejects.
In a report setting out its allegations, Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council said it had recorded 70 attacks between 15 February and 27 October, involving 187 one-way attack drones and 82 munitions dropped or fired from drones.
The council said the attacks had killed or wounded 484 civilians, and killed 176 Sudanese soldiers and wounded another 200.
The report alleged that armed drones had been launching from Ethiopian territory since February 2026 to strike Sudanese cities and civilians. It identified Assosa airport, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area and Bahir Dar air base in Ethiopia’s northwestern Amhara region as launch sites.
According to the council, the campaign accelerated in recent months, with October accounting for 28 attacks and 97 of the one-way attack drones it recorded.
Fresh strikes hit northern power stations
The accusations came as drones struck the Abu Hamad power station in River Nile state and the Ad-Dabba power station in Northern state at dawn on Sunday, according to local reporting. Witnesses described how the attack triggered explosions and a fire at the facility.
Local media said the Ad-Dabba station had been knocked out of service, cutting electricity to the area, and attributed the attack to the RSF.
Drones also reportedly targeted the headquarters of the army’s 73rd Infantry Brigade and two fuel stations in the Al-Multaqa area of Northern state.
The strikes followed several days of attacks on Sudan’s electricity network, with local reporting putting the weekly total of power stations struck this week at 10.
An earlier strike on the Al-Markhiyat substation in Omdurman left large parts of the capital without electricity for more than 12 hours on Tuesday, disrupting hospitals, bakeries and water services. A further attack on Saturday targeted the Hayya power station, which is still under construction in Red Sea state.
Both the Sudanese army and the RSF have used drones during the war, with attacks hitting markets, hospitals, schools, power facilities and displacement camps.
On Monday, an army drone strike on a crowded market in Nyala, the RSF-controlled capital of South Darfur, killed more than 100 people and wounded 113, according to Emergency Lawyers, a rights group. The group said many of the victims were women and children.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the escalating drone attacks on Saturday, saying through his spokesperson that he was "appalled" by their impact on civilians.
"The secretary-general calls on the parties to spare the civilian population and critical infrastructure and agree without delay to a cessation of hostilities as a first step toward ending this devastating conflict," spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.

articles.title: Safety or 'intimidation'? Launch of police unit with military-style rifles sparks human rights fears
articles.body:
IN BRIEF
- The NSW Police's new Armed Response Command officially commenced operations on Sunday.
- Rights advocates have raised concerns that the unit may be used to "intimidate or suppress peaceful protest".
Human rights advocates and political opponents are warning that the NSW Police unit now patrolling Sydney hotspots with military-style rifles could lead to overpolicing and "intimidation".
The $94.3 million, "high-visibility, intelligence-led" Armed Response Command (ARC), which was officially launched on Sunday, was among a range of reforms introduced by the NSW government after the Bondi Beach terror attack on 14 December 2025.
Authorities have said the ARC — a first-of-its-kind rapid response unit in Australia, inspired by similar units in the United Kingdom and Germany — would deter crime, increase community safety, and increase police capacity to respond rapidly to serious threats.
NSW Premier Chris Minns has said: "The security challenges facing our state have changed, and our policing model needs to change with them."
"This is about being prepared for the worst and making sure we can keep the community safe," Minns said when unveiling the ARC in early October.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
NSW Police has said the ARC will increase police presence in "high-risk" areas, including "priority locations, major events, crowded public spaces, sporting matches and places of worship".
The ARC is comprised of 250 "carefully selected officers" who have undergone six months of specialist training, including "rifle proficiency, active armed offender response, advanced driver training and tactical medical care", according to a statement from late October.
The unit, which was announced in late February, will patrol the streets in purpose-built vehicles, fitted with specialised gun safes.
Officers will carry Australian Combat Assault Rifles. Measuring over 70cm long and with a range of more than 500 metres, NSW Police say the weapons were deemed "the most suitable" after "extensive field and endurance testing".
NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon has said the ARC will be "a deterrent for those who wish to commit harm, incite hatred or cause fear".
"The environment in NSW has changed, so the way we police the community has changed and what the community expect from us, has changed," he said on 8 October.
While giving evidence at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, the NSW Police's deputy commissioner said officers responding to the attack at Bondi Beach with standard-issue 9mm Glock pistols were outgunned.
Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin has also said police didn't have the resources to properly respond.
"On December 14 our police were clearly not given the means to promptly stop the attack, and two officers were among the seriously injured as a result," he said.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse."
He said the NSW community should "be grateful to the police and state government" for increasing preparedness, which will "hopefully deter terrorists or end attacks quickly".
ARC an 'escalation of state violence'
However, the unit has also sparked concerns from human rights advocates and some members of the NSW parliament.
Amnesty International Australia has said it has "serious concerns about the increasing militarisation of policing" and is calling for "robust safeguards to protect human rights, particularly the right to peaceful protest".
"People must be able to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly without fear of intimidation or excessive force," Amnesty International Australia strategic campaigner Andrew Witheford said.
"The NSW Government must provide clear assurances that the Armed Response Command will not be used to intimidate or suppress peaceful protest, and ensure its operations are subject to rigorous human rights safeguards and independent scrutiny."
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," he said, adding that the "use of force by police must always comply with international human rights standards".
Sue Higginson, a NSW Greens upper house member and the party's spokesperson for justice, described the ARC as an "intimidation unit" and an "escalation in state violence".
She said police "wav[ing] weapons of death" around Sydney streets would only increase already existing fears of police violence.
"To believe you can intimidate your way to community cohesion is authoritarian and draconian," she added.
"I'm alarmed by the commentary of Commissioner Mal Lanyon that the threat of being shot by police should act as a deterrent to 'harm' or 'hatred'. I am astounded by the attitude of our most senior police officer."
Higginson also raised concerns about how the ARC may seek to use long-range rifles at peaceful protests.
She said that, while political speech has been deemed constitutionally protected from anti-protest laws, it should not be deterred "with guns".
In response to questions about the presence of the ARC at protest events, ARC commander Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said the NSW Police's Public Order and Riot Squad were "the experts when it comes to public order management, not the Armed Response Command".
However, he added that he was "not in a position to say we will never be there".
"If there's information that a particular group might be the target of an active armed offender incident, we will have rifles around the corner," he said at a press conference on Sunday.
NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said the ARC was a "sensible" and "measured" response to events like the Bondi massacre and "nobody is better to deploy this than the New South Wales Police and the officers that we have who are expertly trained".
She added that, since the Bondi attack, there hadn't been "much of a backlash" from the deployment of officers with long-armed rifles at large public events, such as New Year's Eve celebrations in Sydney and Melbourne and at the Sydney Cricket Grounds for the final Ashes Test match in January.
Declining trust in NSW Police
NSW Police has experienced a significant decline in community trust since 2019, according to data from the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research.
Community confidence in the police's ability to bring offenders to justice dropped from 82 per cent in 2019 to 73 per cent in 2025.
Only 49 per cent of respondents felt police dealt with cases promptly, compared to 66 per cent in 2019.
Over the same period, confidence that police officers respected the rights of people accused of crimes declined from 75 to 69 per cent.
Meanwhile, belief that accused persons are treated fairly fell from 77 to 69 per cent and trust that police meet victims' needs dropped from 70 per cent to 56 per cent.
Evans told ARC officers during their attestation that he hoped the unit would improve the community's trust in police.
"When a member of the public sees an ARC vehicle, I want them to feel reassured," he said.

articles.title: Latvia reports brief airspace intrusion near Russia, Belarus borders
articles.body:
RIGA, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Latvia’s armed forces reported a brief intrusion into the country’s airspace near the borders with Belarus and Russia on Sunday, asking people in the area to stay inside for their safety during the incident.
“We inform you that there is a threat in the airspace… If you notice a low-flying or suspicious object, do not approach,” the military said in a post on X. Some 30 minutes later it said the unidentified object had left Latvian airspace and that the threat had ended.
Ukrainian military drones have been straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, creating concerns that the war in Ukraine is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia and its ally Belarus.
As Ukraine attacks Russian Baltic Sea oil shipping ports, some of its drones have missed their targets and led to security warnings in neighbouring countries. In the case of Latvia, it led to a government collapse earlier this year.
Moscow has accused Kyiv of using NATO airspace as cover for attacks, while Kyiv says some of its drones have been steered off course by Russian signal jamming. The NATO countries generally blame Russia for the incidents, for having ignited the war by invading its neighbour nearly five years ago.
(Reporting by Janis Laizans, writing by Terje SolsvikEditing by Hugh Lawson and Peter Graff)

articles.title: Production leap in South Azadegan achieved by launching largest oil processing center
articles.body:
Production leap in South Azadegan achieved by launching largest oil processing center
TEHRAN- Completion of the South Azadegan processing facilities raised West Karun capacity and transformed oil production.
According to a Mehr News Agency reporter, the South Azadegan shared oil field, as one of the country’s largest and most strategic hydrocarbon reserves, plays a vital and irreplaceable role in energy sustainability, strengthening national production, and increasing foreign-currency revenues. This huge oil field in the West Karun region, because of its hydrocarbon reservoirs shared with the neighboring country, has always been at the top priority of Iran’s oil industry upstream and development projects.
Recent developments in the region show that, despite all pressures, comprehensive sanctions, and geopolitical complexities, completion of the value chain from well to processing facilities has opened a new horizon for a leap in the country’s crude oil production. In this framework, full operation of the Central Crude Oil Processing (CTEP) facility at South Azadegan is considered a major milestone in creating sustainable infrastructure for maximum exploitation of the production potential of this strategic field and has brought the oil industry’s roadmap into an accelerated development phase.
During implementation of the first-phase development plans for the South Azadegan oil field, heavy executive and engineering steps were taken so that the recovery factor of this shared field would increase noticeably. During this foundational phase, drilling, completion, and commissioning operations for 203 oil wells were successfully completed, and the field’s production structure was fundamentally organized. The output of these extensive measures has been tangible and accelerated growth in daily production figures; South Azadegan oil production rose from about 130,000 barrels per day at the beginning of the 14th government’s work to more than 183,000 barrels per day. Also, at the time the project was handed over to the new contractor, total oil production from the North and South Azadegan fields together reached 237,000 barrels per day. This change of course and upward production trend proves the strategic importance of stabilizing engineering mechanisms and maximum extraction from shared reservoirs in West Karun.
Full operation of the Central Crude Oil Processing (CTEP) facilities of the South Azadegan project, with four oil processing trains, has made this industrial complex, with a final capacity of 320,000 barrels per day, known as the largest and most complete crude oil processing center in the entire country. Before completion of the initial trains, trains C and D of the project, which entered the operational cycle in Dey last year by order of the President, played an important role in the initial increase in production; the third train was launched on 29 Esfand 1403 and reached stable production on 24 Ordibehesht 1404, and the fourth train was launched on 30 Azar 1404 and entered stable production on 4 Dey. In the next step, completion of the first and second trains (A and B) was pursued from Bahman 1404, accompanied by the successful installation of two ultra-heavy separators, each weighing 102 tons, with a diameter of 6.8 meters and a length of 33 meters. After pre-commissioning, equipment testing, and coordination of systems, with a short four-day shutdown to integrate the control and safety systems of the first and second trains with the third and fourth trains, permission to introduce oil was issued, and finally on 19 Mehr 1405, the full 320,000-barrel oil processing capacity of this center was achieved.
Completion of the South Azadegan central processing project is not merely a local achievement; it is considered mother infrastructure for the entire West Karun basin. With the operationalization of this center’s 320,000-barrel capacity, the cumulative ceiling of oil processing and exploitation capacity in the West Karun oil fields has risen to an exceptional figure of 820,000 barrels per day. Because of its geographical location and advanced process design, this center plays a fundamental role in the region’s oil transfer, processing, and stabilization systems and provides a reliable and sustainable platform for developing the capacity of other satellite and neighboring fields. Taking these developments into account, overall progress of the South Azadegan project has exceeded 80 percent, and the file for the main section of surface oil facilities has been conclusively completed; an achievement obtained through close coordination among the Petroleum Engineering and Development Company, the Petropars Group, the employer, subcontractors, and the country’s technical and engineering bodies.
One of the brightest operational aspects of the South Azadegan field development project has been the uninterrupted and courageous continuation of construction and engineering activities amid the highly dangerous conditions of the 12-day war and the third imposed war. In circumstances where field threats could have led to stagnation of projects, no mandatory stoppage or decline in oil production occurred, and development activities were pursued with full force. During these difficult days, about 30 drilling rigs were active in various fields under management; they were suspended for only about one week and solely to observe strict safety measures, and then quickly resumed. Even in the area of international logistics, although maritime traffic for supplying a limited number of heavy items such as separators faced short delays, project experts, through optimal risk management, did not allow this issue to block the path of progress; as a result, the first and second trains were completed without major delay, and national production remained stable in a great test.
Development in the South Azadegan oil field has not been one-dimensional, and environmental requirements and optimal management of energy resources are at the center of its designs. The associated gas section is the only remaining step of the South Azadegan CTEP project, and all the strength and focus of executive agents is directed toward its rapid completion. Under this plan, associated gas processing and compression facilities will be commissioned, and according to the official schedule, the first train of the gas section will officially join the operational cycle by the end of the current year. With full operation of the gas processing units, this center will be able to collect 200 million standard cubic feet of associated gas daily and, instead of burning it in flares, send it to the NGL 3200 plant for purification and hygienic and industrial use; an action that, in addition to creating major economic value and feeding downstream petrochemical industries, will leave a very positive environmental impact on the atmosphere of the West Karun region.
With the definitive completion of the first phase of South Azadegan development, the next step has begun with a much broader target. From Ordibehesht (April), the second phase of the project for the entire shared Azadegan field (North and South) entered operational phases, including deep engineering studies, process design, holding major tenders, and supplying heavy drilling rigs, advanced downhole pumps, and modern well-completion equipment. Alongside this field development, a balanced and multidimensional development approach is also underway in other West Karun projects; including the Sohrab shared field, where after revision of plans to reduce damage to the Hour al-Azim wetland ecosystem, official environmental permits were issued and operations continued; or the 435-megawatt West Karun power plant, which, while supplying the 100-megawatt needs of the facilities, has provided about 300 megawatts of surplus and stable electricity to the country’s national grid since 1400. In addition, the doors of foreign investment remain open for continued participation of Chinese companies in fields such as Yadavaran and for pursuing development contracts with Russian companies in the Aban, Paydar Gharb, Cheshmeh Khosh, Dalpari, and Paydar Sharq fields—especially in the area of supplying downhole pumps—placing South Azadegan at the top of a chain of wealth creation, industrial independence, and technological synergy.

articles.title: AI reality check triggers $2 trillion tech stock rout
articles.body:
AI reality check triggers $2 trillion tech stock rout
An estimated $2 trillion in market value was wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 during October as investors grow increasingly skeptical that enormous spending on artificial intelligence will ever pay off.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% in its biggest one-day fall since June. Over the whole month, the Nasdaq shed about 5.2%, its worst showing since March 2025, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.2%, and the Dow – which includes many traditional businesses – still finished October up 1.5%.
Among the hardest-hit companies was Google owner Alphabet, whose shares plunged 12.6% on Thursday in its worst day on record. The slump was triggered by its earnings showing slower growth in search advertising, its core business.
While search advertising revenue still grew 12%, Google executive Philipp Schindler acknowledged that its AI Mode brings in less ad revenue per search than traditional results. At the same time, Alphabet is spending heavily on AI infrastructure, putting further pressure on its cash flow. The company’s net profit also slid 25% year-on-year, largely due to investment-related losses, while Thursday’s share plunge erased nearly $500 billion from its market value.
Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the preceding 12 months, largely due to AI investments, with its shares falling 1.4% on Friday. Chipmaker Intel came out worse, plunging 28.6%, its worst day since 1974, after forecasting weaker profits amid trouble in its PC and manufacturing businesses. 
Nvidia – which produces powerful chips used to train and run AI systems – slipped 4.2%, becoming the biggest drag on the S&P 500, while rival AMD dropped 10.9%.
Commenting on the slump, Globalt Investments senior portfolio manager Keith Buchanan, described the current state of the market as “scrutinizing” and “discerning”. “Last year was hope. This year is: At the end of day, how does this all work in real-world terms, like how to finance [it] and who gets the economics. Those questions are much more difficult to answer,” he told CNBC.
Enormous spending on AI and data centers has become a staple of US tech giants in recent years. Together, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet are projected to spend more than $700 billion on data centers, computing equipment and other long-term investments in 2026 alone, and much of it is AI-related.
According to various estimates, global AI-related investment is valued at between $900 billion and $2.7 trillion dollars this year, depending on the methodology. Companies are also borrowing more to finance expansion, fueling concerns among investors.
Market analysts meanwhile warn of further near-term losses. Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett expects weakness until mid-November, while Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson says the S&P 500 could fall even further within weeks before recovering by year-end.
Other major tests for the US market are the midterm elections on Tuesday, which could reshape AI regulation, as well as quarterly results from Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Palantir, and Friday’s jobs report.

articles.title: Tehran, New Delhi hold talks to deepen ties in technology sector
articles.body:
Tehran, New Delhi hold talks to deepen ties in technology sector
TEHRAN – Iran and India have discussed ways to expand cooperation in information and communication technology (ICT), promote specialized exchanges, and strengthen coordination in international forums.
ICT Minister Sattar Hashemi and India’s Ambassador to Iran, Vishwesh Negi, held a meeting on Saturday to explore the two countries’ capacities for joint initiatives in the sector, Mehr News Agency reported.
 
The discussions focused on identifying opportunities for cooperation between government bodies and private-sector ICT stakeholders, enhancing professional interactions, and making greater use of the two countries’ scientific, technical, and technological capabilities.
Given the respective capacities and the regional and international standing of Iran and India, both parties underlined the need for the promotion of cooperation and coordination within specialized international forums and organizations, particularly those related to the ICT sector.
The officials also highlighted the importance of harmonizing views, participating in ongoing consultations, and strengthening joint initiatives to ensure a more effective presence on the international stage.
The two sides agreed to continue discussions, follow up on the discussed issues, and enhance ties in areas of mutual interest.
Tech ties with India in key sectors
In February, Hashemi, in a meeting with Indian Minister of Electronics and Information Technology, Jitin Prasada, voiced the country’s readiness for the expansion of scientific and technological ties with India in key sectors, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, and the digital economy.
The officials met on the sidelines of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, being conducted in person at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from February 16 to 20, IRIB reported.
During the meeting, Hashemi highlighted the capabilities of the two sides in emerging technologies. Referring to Iran’s strong scientific and human infrastructure, he said the country has taken great strides in advancing modern technologies.
The official went on to say that India is one of the global hubs for software development, a powerful country with high capacity in developing and exporting IT, cybersecurity, and AI. So, promoting technological ties between the two countries will lead to the formation of a digital powerhouse.
According to Hashemi, enhancing interactions between the private sectors is among the top priorities. “We are interested in developing operational cooperation in large language models (LLMs), the development of an AI joint platform in the agriculture sector, and the establishment of innovative centers to utilize AI in different fields,” he said.
Highlighting the importance of securing critical infrastructure in the years ahead and India’s capacity in training specialized human resources, Hashemi announced Iran’s readiness to share experiences in cyber threats, combating emerging malware, and strengthening the security of financial infrastructure.
The ICT minister also proposed developing a joint fund to support Iranian and Indian startups, holding joint technological events, and talent exchange programs, allocating special zones in the technology parks of the two countries, and facilitating the issuance of ‘tech visas’ for IT professionals as practical ways to foster cooperation.
For his part, Prasada underscored expanding collaboration between the two sides, saying that India is willing to expand ties with Iran via sharing expertise in AI and cybersecurity, holding workshops on training specialized human resources, and kicking off operational cooperation in collaborative technological projects.
“Establishing joint innovation centers and exchanging experts would help accelerate technological development in both countries, strengthen digital infrastructure, and improve data security,” Prasada noted.

articles.title: Iran designates MI6, Royal Navy and RAF under reciprocal measures against UK
articles.body:
Iran designates MI6, Royal Navy and RAF under reciprocal measures against UK
TEHRAN — Iran has announced reciprocal measures against the United Kingdom, designating its foreign intelligence service, MI6, as a hostile group and its Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations, in response to 'Britain's unlawful and hostile actions against the Islamic Republic.'
In a statement issued on Sunday, November 1, Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the British government's anti-Iranian policies, saying they violated the principles of the United Nations Charter and international law, particularly respect for national sovereignty and the prohibition of unlawful measures against other countries.
The ministry said the measures were intended to safeguard Iran's national security and interests and reaffirmed the government's determination to take all necessary steps to protect the country.
According to the statement, the decision was adopted in response to British actions over the past year, including the country's involvement in the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran through the provision of military bases, facilities and logistical support.
The ministry also cited Britain's decision on July 13, 2026, to bring Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) under the State Threats Act 2026 as part of the grounds for the reciprocal measures.
The Foreign Ministry said the measures were based on a resolution adopted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council and took effect upon publication of the statement on November 1.
Under the decision, Britain's Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as MI6, has been designated a hostile group pursuant to Note 2 of Article 1 of Iran's law on intensifying penalties for espionage and cooperation with the Zionist regime and hostile countries against national security and interests.
The Royal Navy and Royal Air Force, meanwhile, have been placed under Iran's law on reciprocal action against the United States' designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization and will accordingly be recognized as terrorist organizations.
The ministry emphasized that the measures were adopted in accordance with international law and the principle of reciprocity, holding the British government responsible for any consequences arising from its actions.
The decision comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and London over Britain's role in the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran and its subsequent measures against the IRGC.
Iran has consistently maintained that the provision of military facilities and logistical support for attacks against its territory constitutes a violation of its sovereignty and international law. Tehran has also condemned the designation of the IRGC by Western governments as an interference in its internal affairs and a hostile act against the country's national security.
By extending reciprocal measures to British intelligence and military institutions, Iran has signaled that it will respond to actions it considers hostile through its own legal and security framework.
The Foreign Ministry's statement concluded by reiterating that the British government would bear responsibility for the consequences of its policies and actions against Iran.

Russia's FSB says minor detained over park attack threat after US tip-off
Nov 1 - Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said on Sunday that a Russian minor had been detained over a threat to carry out a terrorist attack in a Moscow park following a tip-off from the United States, news agency Interfax reported.
On Saturday, the FSB said it had received information from the US through established partner channels about preparations for an attack in Moscow and was taking appropriate measures.
The minor had posted photographs of himself on TikTok wearing tactical clothing and a balaclava, holding an object that looked like an automatic weapon, as well as photographs taken at Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve with the caption: "I found a place," Interfax cited the FSB as saying.
"We are grateful to the American side for providing the information," the security service was quoted as saying in its statement.
It said officials searching the minor's home found the clothes and accessories seen in the social media posts, while his phone showed a subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the app Telegram and “a significant number of searches concerning terrorist attacks, mass killings and other acts of violence,” according to Interfax.
Russia's Investigative Committee is considering what legal or procedural action to take, the FSB said.
Tsaritsyno, a palace museum and park complex in southern Moscow, was temporarily closed on Saturday following the US tip-off. REUTERS

Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, said the remaining 10 percent of tokens are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
The company said it has set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in the hack.
Binance said Friday it was working to resolve what it called a "complex attack" with several "points of breach."
North Korea link
Later on Saturday, the FBI said that North Korea was behind the theft.
"The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the US law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the incident, but said in its latest update they were on track to resume on Sunday.
The attack on Binance came as many observers expressed worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

- China called the report “groundless speculation”, while the case highlights wider US-China tensions over chips, AI policy and Beijing’s tech ambitions.

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump voiced on Oct 31 his support for the “brilliant” head of US chip giant Nvidia, Jensen Huang, after a report that he was targeted by a Chinese spy plot.
Trump said the US was looking “very closely” at the issue.
The New York Times reported on Oct 29 that US intelligence officials concluded that a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, who had interacted with Huang, had been funnelling information to Beijing.
China has dismissed the report as “groundless speculation”.
“I have a lot of respect for Jensen. I didn’t know about the specific thing, but I hope he’s going to be OK. He’s a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people,” Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
“We’re going to check it out very closely,” he added.
Asked if he would retain Huang as an adviser, he said: “I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary, I’ve always found Jensen Huang to be very above board.”
“But you know, you’re dealing in a very complex issue,” he added.
Huang has advised Trump on AI policy and was among tech CEOs who joined the US leader on his visit to Beijing in May to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The Taiwan-born businessman has advocated for the use of his company’s chips in China, where Beijing has been accelerating development of its own semiconductors. AFP

articles.title: Drone strike hits power station in northern Sudan as attacks on energy facilities mount
articles.body:
A drone strike hit a power station in northern Sudan early on Sunday, sparking a fire and triggering loud explosions, witnesses told Anadolu.
The attack targeted the Abu Hamad power station in River Nile state, about 334 miles (538 kilometres) north of the capital, Khartoum, according to witnesses.
They said loud explosions were heard around the facility as flames engulfed parts of the station.
Videos circulated by activists on social media showed a large fire at the power station.
The latest strike brought to 12 the number of power stations targeted by drone attacks across six Sudanese states since Monday.
The affected states include Khartoum, Gezira, Sennar, Gedaref, River Nile and Red Sea.
There was no immediate comment from Sudanese authorities on the attack or the extent of casualties and damage.
Power infrastructure targeted in series of drone strikes
The latest attack followed another drone strike on Saturday targeting the Hayya power station in Red Sea state, a facility still under construction.
The attacks on power infrastructure come amid the ongoing conflict between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The two sides have been fighting since April 2023, when disagreements over the integration of the country's military forces escalated into armed conflict.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, amid a worsening humanitarian and hunger crisis.

articles.title: Protestors loot shops in Frankfurt
articles.body:
Protestors loot shops in Frankfurt
320,000 hold protests in France as police arrest 770
Protestors looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannons to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles, BBC said on its website.
Thousands joined demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organized by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.
Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organizers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden."
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.
The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
"We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard.
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Similar instances took place in other German cities.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.
Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
French protest organizers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.
